# The instrument design guide

`voice.md`'s sibling: that guide governs what a visitor reads, this one
governs what they see and press. It exists for the same reason — the design
drifts, and it drifts toward decoration. Every element on a demo earns its
place by answering one question: does this contribute to clarity? The page's
feel is a developer environment, not a course platform. Engineer, not
student.

The audience is four people at once — an aspiring developer, a non-technical
visitor, a junior, a senior — and they get **one experience legible at all
levels, never per-level modes**. When a value needs to reach all four, encode
it redundantly (two channels, one display), don't fork the interface.

---

## 1. The fixed grammar

Every demo sits in the same chassis, zones in fixed positions — like a car's
cockpit or an editor's panes, a visitor who has used one instrument has used
them all:

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ● live                        SLOW MOTION ⭘ │  chrome: state left, view right
│                                              │
│  bake #64f93b                                │  the specimen
│  provenance rows · one narration caption     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ [ actions, in execution order ]              │  the deck
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ▸ bake.ts + actions.ts       docs ↗ source ↗ │  reference bar
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **Chrome, top-left — the state gauge.** `live` (cyan) at rest, `working`
  (amber) while any server round trip is out. One in-flight signal per
  instrument; this is it.
- **Chrome, top-right — view controls.** Mode switches (slow motion) live in
  the corner every editor keeps its view switches. Actions never live here.
  Empty when a demo has no alternate view.
- **Body — the specimen.** The observed value large, provenance rows as one
  aligned table, one narration caption. All describing text in one place.
- **Deck — actions only.** Execution order, left to right. When a flow has
  real sequence, the controls diagram it (numbered steps, an arrow, the later
  step dark until the earlier one fires). A deck may end in a **result chip —
  output, never input** — when the platform's own label for the sequence's
  outcome is knowable by rule (exhibit 02: `revalidated · tag-based
  deletion`, the badge Vercel files the refill under).
- **Reference bar — the status bar every editor ends in.** The code drawer's
  disclosure left (source opens inside the chassis, native `<details>`, zero
  JS); `docs` and `source` links pinned right, positioned so clicking them
  never toggles the drawer. Row height mirrors the chrome header.

What the grammar deliberately lacks: a panel label (the intro prose names the
subject once) and a readout footer (the source in the drawer is the spec
plate — a reader who wants identifiers is the reader who opens it).

Outside the chassis: the eyebrow names the chapter and its topic (`the
cache · caching & revalidation`) where engineers read identifiers — two
names, no numeral. Asides are set as `/* code comments */` in comment-gray
mono, because that is what they are.

## 2. Feedback

Anything in flight says so three ways: the gauge flips to `working`, the
specimen dims and pulses, and when the new value lands it takes one amber
wash (`.ht-land` — key-remount, skips first paint, reduced-motion safe) and
settles. No silent updates, ever.

A change spent behind a turning card was never spent. Where a demo hides
its own output while narrating — the state card flips to its source and
back — the face holds the old value for the length of the replay and
changes it only when the front is square to the reader again. The state
itself updates on the click frame, as it always did; what waits is the
display, and the aside under the card is where that gap is stated. The
reveal wears both marks at once, from the one commit: the landing wash
(the value is the key, so the remount plays it) and `.ht-settle`, 420ms,
the digits alone rising a hair into place. The eye's last movement is to
the thing that moved.

The React rule underneath: **client-owned state paints on the click frame;
only the server sync lives in a transition.** A mode flip inside the same
transition as its `router.refresh()` freezes the control until the round
trip resolves. While the flipped view waits for the server, the copy must
narrate the in-flight window honestly rather than claim a state the screen
doesn't show (see the settling readout in `rebake-copy.ts`).

## 3. Copy and demo co-evolve

A demo that gains a capability can obsolete prose that was accurate the day
it shipped — voice.md's three passes check a line against the panel *as it
is*, so re-run them whenever the panel changes. (Evidence: voice.md §6,
2026-08-19.)

---
name: hastoggle-positioning-decisions
description: Current positioning (2026-07 pivot) — live playground for Next.js & Vercel; supersedes the 2026-04 AI-ownership landing thesis
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: d48f16f7-831b-4c9f-9fb8-661aab374da6
  modified: 2026-08-21T07:13:02.280Z
---

**PIVOT (2026-07-31):** Eric reconsidered the 2026-04 AI-misconceptions direction. hasToggle.dev is now **the live playground for Next.js & Vercel** — interactive demos of real features running on the page itself, aiming to eventually cover "everything Next.js has to offer" plus as much of the Vercel platform as can be demoed from a page. Audience: bootcamp grads → seniors (Eric's bootcamp-coach background is the trust anchor). The old landing (5 misconception demos, three-moves/Values, misconceptions route) was deleted; the masterclass and learn pages survive unlinked.

**Funnel (locked):** weekly digest form (kept — email capture is load-bearing) promising "one new exhibit every Monday", and **paid small cohorts** where Eric coaches; cohort seats announced to the list first. Playground itself stays free, permanently.

**Built-in-public angle:** repo is public; the site is built with AI (Conductor driving Claude Code) and the process is published via Entire.io as part of the curriculum. "The site is its own biggest demo." (Checkpoints repo is public since 2026-08-20 and linked from the landing page and lab chapter making-of strips.)

**Three-layer model (2026-08-21, Eric's articulation — direction, mostly settled):**
1. **The lab** (`/lab`, built) — live running references, mechanism-truth,
   audience-agnostic, a destination. The demos are their own abstraction
   layer.
2. **Learning paths** (`/learn` territory) — narrative, goal-directed
   routes through the lab's landmarks, shaped per audience (beginner /
   junior / senior crossing over) and per *constraint* (e.g. the feature
   inside a multi-tenant app — "the feature within a constrained
   environment"). Open question whether cohort-gated or public; **Eric
   leans public**, not formally settled.
3. **The cohort** — paid structured experience that *relies on* existing
   demos and paths, adds recorded video or live streams; where
   comprehensive ground-up web development gets taught, depending on the
   cohort run.
The boundary rule that fell out of discussion: the lab doesn't know who's
reading; a path knows exactly who's reading. design.md's four-audience /
no-per-level-modes rule is the lab's half of that contract. Existing
/learn content is proto-specimens of the other layers (ref-vs-state,
qa-stories, parked Hazel counter = path lessons; the masterclass = a
cohort-layer artifact whose beat transport could become the path
sequencing primitive).

**What carried over from the old positioning:** the three-layer voice (Surface plain / Meta Pratchett-dry `MetaAside` asides / Demo reveals), the editorial design system (Switzer + JetBrains Mono, plus-grid, ht-cyan, § dividers, numbered-chapter Contents), and the "real, not simulated" demo ethic. The Wittgenstein/ownership thesis and "three moves" copy are retired from the page; don't resurrect them in new copy.

**Technical positioning choice (2026-07-31):** apps/web runs `cacheComponents: true` — the landing page teaches the current Next 16 model (use cache / cacheLife / cacheTag / updateTag / PPR / Suspense streaming) by running it on itself. First five exhibits: boundary (server vs client), shell (re-bake this page), stream, mutation (cookie counter), image (/api/og). Roadmap section lists ~10 upcoming exhibits; "new exhibit every Monday" is the content cadence Eric committed to on-page.

**How to apply:** new landing copy and demos serve the playground thesis (show, don't tell; real behavior with honest readouts; link official docs from every exhibit). Cohort/digest copy stays no-asterisk honest about what's paid.
---
name: lab-architecture
description: "Approved 2026-08-20 — /lab is the playground's home; serialized-book shape, syllabus registry, chapter pages; landing becomes the front door"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: c0f2ba34-9617-46d3-8ed5-02645177a756
  modified: 2026-08-20T19:48:19.010Z
---

Eric approved the playground architecture on 2026-08-20 ("lab is perfect"):
a serialized web book whose chapters run. `/[locale]/lab` is the contents
page; each exhibit owns `/[locale]/lab/<slug>` (route segments, so
route-shaped topics — parallel routes, not-found, params, view transitions —
can exist at all). A single `syllabus.ts` registry (n, slug, topic,
navLabel, belief, status, shippedOn) drives contents rows, the landing
roadmap, ContentsNav, prev/next, sitemap, OG titles, and a `/latest`
redirect. Approved with it: canonical pages for the five landing exhibits
(extracted wrappers, landing unchanged), live per-row values on the
contents page (bounded, Suspense-streamed, truth rule: per-visitor values
say so). Rejected: doc-site shell, single growing page, /exhibits (museum
word), /poke, /proof. "Lab" is rooted in the shipped FAQ line "the lab
bench that belongs next to them"; the address is a noun, "poking" stays
the verb. Prose migration decided same day ("landing page should use lab as
well") and shipped: visitor prose says "chapter"/"the lab" everywhere
(landing, FAQ, /confirmed, OG card); "exhibit" survives only as internal
vocabulary in code comments and docs. Built 2026-08-20 in PR #392, six
slices, all verified on production builds; decisions recorded in
voice.md §6 and design.md §4 ("The lab — site shape"). Build contract in
the kinshasa workspace at `.context/lab-design.md` (untracked). Related:
[[hastoggle-positioning]], [[playground-design-language]].

content.text:
I read the web app, both docs, the syllabus registry, the landing/lab/FAQ copy, and the positioning memories. Here's what I'd write, and why.

## What the current README gets wrong

It's untouched next-forge boilerplate. It describes a repo that doesn't exist any more: `npx next-forge@latest init`, a Mintlify docs app (`apps/docs` is an empty shell), "type-safe ORM with migrations" (it's raw MongoDB, no ORM, no migrations), demo links to `demo.next-forge.com`, and a vercel/next-forge contributing guide + contributors image. Nothing in it mentions the actual product. Anyone landing from the checkpoints repo learns nothing.

## Who the README is for

The repo is public *as part of the product* — the landing page and every chapter's making-of strip link to it. So the README's job is not "how to install a SaaS template." It's: what hasToggle is, where the interesting code lives, how to run it, and where it's headed. next-forge becomes a credit line near the bottom, not the headline.

## Proposed structure

**1. Title + standfirst** — `hasToggle.dev`, "The unofficial live playground for Next.js and Vercel." Then the three facts that matter: everything runs, the source is in every panel, the process is published.

**2. What it is** — the lab as a serialized web book whose chapters run. Each chapter opens on a belief a developer holds ("I'll put `use client` on it, to be safe") and runs the real feature next to it. Free permanently; the paid thing is cohort coaching. Not affiliated with Vercel.

**3. What's running** — a table of the six shipped chapters (belief · topic · route), plus what lands next Monday, with a pointer that `syllabus.ts` is the source of truth and this table is a snapshot.

**4. Where the interesting code is** — the section a repo visitor actually came for. `apps/web/app/[locale]/(playground)/*` (one folder per chapter, demo + source + index-value), `lab/syllabus.ts` (one registry driving contents rows, roadmap, page-turns, sitemap, OG, `/latest`), `api/og`, `docs/voice.md` and `docs/design.md` as the two governing documents.

**5. Running it** — `bun install`, `MONGODB_URI`, `turbo dev --filter=web` on 3001. Plus the one non-obvious warning worth putting in a README: `next dev` lies about cache semantics, so preview deploys are the truth-bench for anything touching `use cache`.

**6. How it's built** — Conductor orchestrating Claude Code, every prompt and checkpoint published to the checkpoints repo, `CLAUDE.md` as the agent's instructions, tests/Biome/typecheck as the gates.

**7. Where this is going** — the two milestones, below.

**8. Inherited from next-forge** — credit, what's still in use (Turborepo layout, `packages/*`, Biome/ultracite), what's diverged (MongoDB, better-auth, the web app entirely). License.

### Sample of the opening, for voice

> # hasToggle.dev
>
> **The unofficial live playground for Next.js and Vercel.**
>
> Every chapter opens on something developers say — *"I'll put `use client` on it, to be safe"*, *"It's either cached or it isn't"* — and runs the real feature next to it. Not a screenshot of the feature, not a sandbox running a copy: the page you are reading is the thing being demonstrated. Press the button, watch the cache expire, open the drawer and read the code that did it.
>
> The site is live at [hasToggle.dev](https://hastoggle.dev). This repo is the whole of it, and [a second repo](https://github.com/hasToggle/hasToggle.dev-checkpoints) publishes every prompt and checkpoint that produced it.

A README is repo chrome, not marketing chrome — so I'd keep it plainer than the landing page: no hero pastiche, no `//` asides, and the instrument register only where it's naming real identifiers. I'd rather it read as the honest technical document that the site's authority rests on. Say the word if you want it warmer.

## The two milestones, as I'd record them

I'd give them a `## Where this is going` section — two named milestones, each with the forcing fact that makes it non-obvious, so the section is a commitment rather than a wish list.

> ### 1. The full range
>
> The syllabus is the whole of what Next.js can do, plus as much of Vercel as can be proved from inside a web page. Six chapters are running; twenty-odd topics still wear a `+`. The milestone is the day the `+` rows run out — routing in all its forms, the asset pipeline, the edge, cron, storage, rollbacks. One chapter a week, in whatever order the work happens.
>
> ### 2. The shop
>
> A production application that is meta about its own implementation: a real (if fictional) ecommerce site, with a table of contents per page and per section listing every mechanism that page is made of. Click any piece of content and the site shows you what's underneath it — which cache holds it, which boundary it crossed, which route rendered it.
>
> The reason this is a separate milestone and not more chapters: **a production site is where features interact, and interaction is the one thing an isolated demo cannot show.** A chapter can prove that `use cache` refills on a tag. It cannot show you what happens when that cache sits behind an intercepted route, under a Server Action that also writes a cookie, on a page whose OG image is generated from the same data. The shop is where the chapters meet each other.

Three things I'd flag rather than decide, because they're design calls:

- **What it's called and where it lives.** `/shop` is honest and boring; something like `/floor` or `/store` keeps the place-noun principle that gave `/lab` its name. It's a third top-level surface next to the lab and the paths — worth naming deliberately.
- **The inspector is a new instrument.** "Click any content, see its mechanism" is not the fixed chassis in `design.md` §1 — it's an overlay that annotates arbitrary page regions. That's a real design round, and it's the hard part of the milestone.
- **Whether the TOC is authored or derived.** The lab's whole discipline is that one registry drives every list. A hand-written mechanism list per page would be the first thing on the site that can silently go stale. Deriving it — from the modules a page actually renders — is harder and much more in character.

Want me to write the README now, or adjust the framing first? I can also open the milestone-2 shape as a proper design round in `.context/` rather than letting the README be the only place it's specified.

name: project-ts7-migration
description: "TypeScript 7 (native/tsgo) migration state, the native-preview shim, and what CI actually is on hasToggle.dev"
metadata:

TS 7 migration (PR #284, renovate/typescript-7.x, 2026-07-10): typescript@7.0.2 is the native Go compiler — the JS compiler API (`typescript/lib/typescript.js`) no longer ships. Next.js 16 stable can't load it (vercel/next.js#95490; fix is canary-only behind `experimental.useTypeScriptCli`).

**Shim in place:** `@typescript/native-preview` root devDep exists ONLY as a marker so `next build` takes its graceful native-compiler path and skips build-time type checking. Type safety is instead gated by the turbo `typecheck` task (native `tsc --noEmit`), which `build` depends on. **Remove the marker + its renovate.json exclusion rule once Next stable supports typescript@7 natively.**

Renovate-hardening (Eric's explicit requirement: future Renovate PRs must keep passing typechecks): the marker package is excluded in renovate.json (nightly churn), and `packages/payments` no longer pins Stripe's `apiVersion` literal — the SDK default is always in sync with its own types, so stripe bumps can't desync them again.

Non-obvious repo facts learned then:
- "CI" = the Vercel deploy of `apps/web` (has-toggle-dev-web) + Claude review actions. No GitHub Actions build/test; app/api local builds fail on missing Clerk env vars (pre-existing, unrelated to deps).
- `bun run check` (ultracite@latest) is broken locally/on main: "Could not resolve ultracite/core" — pre-existing, not in CI.
- tsup `dts` is disabled (needs the removed TS JS API); tsup is unmaintained, tsdown is the successor if the CLI ever needs .d.ts again.
- Official TS6-API escape hatch if a tool needs the old API: alias `"typescript": "npm:@typescript/typescript6"` + `"@typescript/native": "npm:typescript@7"`.
- CLAUDE.md is stale re: database (says Prisma/Neon; package actually uses mongodb, no schema.prisma).
---
name: project-env-quirks
description: "Machine/env quirks on Eric's Mac that bite headless agent sessions (docker pulls, biome gate)"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: b10586c9-1b13-412f-92b7-ddd260a6528c
  modified: 2026-08-21T05:23:32.243Z
---

Two environment quirks hit during the knowledge-hub build (2026-07-11):

1. **`docker pull` hangs forever in headless sessions.** `~/.docker/config.json` has `credsStore: "desktop"` plus a Docker Scout hook on `pull`; the credential helper blocks on macOS Keychain without a UI. Even `docker run` hangs at "Unable to find image locally".
   **How to apply:** `mkdir -p /tmp/docker-nocreds && echo '{}' > /tmp/docker-nocreds/config.json`, then `DOCKER_CONFIG=/tmp/docker-nocreds docker pull …` — completes in seconds. `docker ps`/`exec`/`run` (with image present) work normally.

2. **Biome gate (ultracite v7 extends paths): fixed per-branch, not repo-wide.** biome.jsonc must extend `ultracite/biome/*` (v7 layout), not the v5-era `ultracite/core|react|next`; check/fix scripts must run the local ultracite pin, never `@latest`. Applied on Kheirah/agent-knowledge-hub-design (484e1a0 + 26327a7, 2026-07-11) and independently re-derived on Kheirah/continue-prev-task (fe73b90, 2026-07-12) — branches cut before those commits will still show "Could not resolve ultracite/core"; apply the same two-line fix. Repo-wide pre-existing findings remain (hundreds; scoped `bunx biome check <path>` is the usable gate for new work). The masterclass exhibit dir is mechanically clean as of fe73b90 (~36 judgment-rule findings left: noJsxPropsBind, noExportedImports, index keys).
   **Zombie dirty files:** entire.io (manual-commit strategy) snapshots uncommitted changes to a shadow branch and re-applies them post-commit ("carried forward remaining files") — a plain `git checkout --` of unwanted noise gets silently undone at the next commit. Cure: `git checkout -- <files> && entire clean --force` (drops the HEAD shadow branch + session carry-forward state; committed checkpoint history is unaffected).
   Also: Biome's `useSortedKeys` assist auto-sorts object keys on `--write` — it silently reorders semantically-ordered literals (MongoDB compound-index key specs). Guard such files with `// biome-ignore-all assist/source/useSortedKeys: …`.

3. **Vercel:** hasToggle.dev deploys as project `has-toggle-dev-web` under team scope `spiritsdontfly` (not the default `kheirahs-projects`, not `forsuxess`). Use `vercel ls/inspect --scope spiritsdontfly`; `vercel inspect --logs <url>` pulls build logs without switching scope. (2026-07-24)

4. **Bun override staleness:** after adding a root `overrides` entry, plain `bun install` updates `bun.lock` but can leave stale `.bun` store symlinks (nested dep still resolving to the old version). `rm -rf node_modules && bun install` is required for the override to actually take effect. (2026-07-24, radix-slot pin)

5. **The `web` app's locale-prefixed URLs 500 in dev.** `http://localhost:3001/en/learn/...` dies in middleware (`[NEMO] Middleware execution failed`); the unprefixed `http://localhost:3001/learn/...` serves fine. Use the unprefixed path when driving the site in a browser or the masterclass page looks broken when it isn't. `curl` also 500s on both (the middleware chain needs real browser headers) — verify with Playwright/Chrome DevTools, not curl. Next 16 also refuses to start a second dev server for the same project dir ("Run kill <pid> to stop it"), so reuse Eric's running server on 3001 rather than starting your own. (2026-07-25)

6. **Shared `.next` dir: `next build` then `next dev` corrupts some routes.** Running dev after a prod build in the same `apps/web/.next` produces `SyntaxError: Unexpected non-whitespace character after JSON` and 500s on a subset of routes (hit the nuqs-using learn pages, 2026-07-31, Next 16.2 + cacheComponents) while others serve fine. Cure: `rm -rf apps/web/.next` before starting dev. Don't misread the 500s as an app bug — the prod build of the same source passes.

7. **`vercel link` writes into `apps/web/.env.local` — never `rm` that file.** The CLI appends a `VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN` and reports "✓ Updated .env.local", so the file looks like a linking artifact when it is actually Eric's pre-existing local env (2846 bytes, gitignored, unrecoverable from git). A subagent ran `rm -rf .vercel .env.local` as "cleanup" and destroyed it (2026-08-10).
   **How to apply:** clean up after `vercel link` with `rm -rf apps/web/.vercel` only. If the env file is already gone, restore it from the source repo — `cp -p /Users/eric/Projects/hasToggle/hasToggle.dev/apps/web/.env.local apps/web/` — which is where Conductor seeds workspace copies from; the OIDC token is ephemeral and regenerates. Tell agents driving Vercel not to touch `.env.local` at all.

8. **Preview deploys are SSO-protected**, so `curl`/Playwright get an auth wall. Vercel's Protection Bypass for Automation is the documented way through — but it mints secrets that must be revoked afterwards, so verify revocation in the dashboard rather than trusting an agent's report. (2026-08-10)

9. **Cache-invalidation behaviour does not reproduce in `next dev`.** `updateTag` in dev goes through a tiered cache handler (built-in front handler paired with the real one, `server/use-cache/handlers.js`), so a `use cache` entry written during a server action survives a reload — on Vercel it does not, because the tag's expiry watermark is stamped after the render that wrote it. Anything testing `use cache` / `updateTag` / revalidation semantics must be verified on a preview deploy; a clean dev run proves nothing. (2026-08-10, landing-page shell demo)

10. **React DevTools extension throws spurious console errors on the rebake demo.** "The children should not have changed if we pass in the same set." with a stack entirely inside `chrome-extension://…/installHook.js` — the extension's fiber-mirror desyncs on transition commits with RSC children props + keyed remounts. Not an app bug: absent in extension-free browsers, string doesn't exist in React/Next/Radix bundles. Diagnose via `apps/web/.next/dev/logs/next-development.log` (timestamps are server *uptime*, not wall clock). (2026-08-19)

11. **`bun test` is not the full gate — it does not typecheck.** Vercel's build runs `bun run typecheck` (tsc) per workspace and fails on what bun test happily passes (e.g. a state-type gaining a required field while test literals lag: broke the build 2026-08-20). Before pushing any type-shape change: `cd apps/web && bun test && bun run typecheck`.

12. **Run `bun test` from inside the workspace dir, never the repo root.** Root `bun test` sweeps up every workspace's tests without their per-workspace `bunfig.toml` preloads, so `apps/web`'s fetch mocks are missing (`undefined is not an object (evaluating 'response.ok')` in email-validation tests) and mongodb throws an unhandled v8-snapshot error. The false failures look like regressions in files you never touched, and the test/file counts jump (189/30 → 208/34 was the tell, 2026-08-19). The usable gates: `cd apps/web && bun test`, or `turbo test --filter=web`.

13. **Lighthouse's default (simulated/Lantern) throttling is meaningless against `localhost`.** Because a local server has ~0 latency, every resource finishes inside the observed paint, so Lantern's pessimistic LCP graph charges LCP for the page's *entire* byte weight — LCP reads ~5s while the observed value is ~90ms and `observedFCP === observedLCP`. The number barely moves no matter what you cut (removing a 1.9s streaming hold, or all of Sentry, each shifted it <0.5s). Always add `--throttling-method=devtools` (real throttling) when benchmarking a local `next start`; on the landing page that was the difference between 80 and 100. Confirmed by the observed-vs-simulated fields in `audits.metrics.details.items[0]`. (2026-08-20)

14. **Fade-in entrance animations defer LCP by their full delay+duration.** An element animating `opacity: 0 → 1` is not a paint the browser counts, so LCP lands at `FCP + delay + duration` — the hero's `ht-enter` (80ms + 700ms) put LCP exactly 780ms after FCP in every run. Animating `transform` only, at full opacity (`ht-enter-opaque`/`ht-slide` in `apps/web/app/styles.css`), keeps the motion and makes the paint count immediately. Check this before blaming bundle size. (2026-08-20)

15. **Tailwind `scroll-smooth` on `<html>` needs `data-scroll-behavior="smooth"` beside it (Next 16).** The router's `disableSmoothScrollDuringRouteTransition` only suppresses CSS smooth scrolling during route-transition scroll resets when the html element carries the data attribute — it won't pay `getComputedStyle` to detect the CSS, and in production there's no warning. Without it every client-side navigation animates its scroll-to-top from the old position (~900ms of the new page sliding up); hash/anchor scrolls are exempt either way, so the glide survives the fix. Bit the lab pages 2026-08-21 (invisible before — the landing page had only anchor scrolls); fixed in `apps/web/app/layout.tsx` on Kheirah/playground-site-design.

TS 7 migration (PR #284, renovate/typescript-7.x, 2026-07-10): typescript@7.0.2 is the native Go compiler — the JS compiler API (`typescript/lib/typescript.js`) no longer ships. Next.js 16 stable can't load it (vercel/next.js#95490; fix is canary-only behind `experimental.useTypeScriptCli`).

**Shim in place:** `@typescript/native-preview` root devDep exists ONLY as a marker so `next build` takes its graceful native-compiler path and skips build-time type checking. Type safety is instead gated by the turbo `typecheck` task (native `tsc --noEmit`), which `build` depends on. **Remove the marker + its renovate.json exclusion rule once Next stable supports typescript@7 natively.**

Renovate-hardening (Eric's explicit requirement: future Renovate PRs must keep passing typechecks): the marker package is excluded in renovate.json (nightly churn), and `packages/payments` no longer pins Stripe's `apiVersion` literal — the SDK default is always in sync with its own types, so stripe bumps can't desync them again.

Non-obvious repo facts learned then:
- "CI" = the Vercel deploy of `apps/web` (has-toggle-dev-web) + Claude review actions. No GitHub Actions build/test; app/api local builds fail on missing Clerk env vars (pre-existing, unrelated to deps).
- `bun run check` (ultracite@latest) is broken locally/on main: "Could not resolve ultracite/core" — pre-existing, not in CI.
- tsup `dts` is disabled (needs the removed TS JS API); tsup is unmaintained, tsdown is the successor if the CLI ever needs .d.ts again.
- Official TS6-API escape hatch if a tool needs the old API: alias `"typescript": "npm:@typescript/typescript6"` + `"@typescript/native": "npm:typescript@7"`.
- CLAUDE.md is stale re: database (says Prisma/Neon; package actually uses mongodb, no schema.prisma).

name: project-env-quirks
description: "Machine/env quirks on Eric's Mac that bite headless agent sessions (docker pulls, biome gate)"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: b10586c9-1b13-412f-92b7-ddd260a6528c
  modified: 2026-08-21T05:23:32.243Z
---

Two environment quirks hit during the knowledge-hub build (2026-07-11):

1. **`docker pull` hangs forever in headless sessions.** `~/.docker/config.json` has `credsStore: "desktop"` plus a Docker Scout hook on `pull`; the credential helper blocks on macOS Keychain without a UI. Even `docker run` hangs at "Unable to find image locally".
   **How to apply:** `mkdir -p /tmp/docker-nocreds && echo '{}' > /tmp/docker-nocreds/config.json`, then `DOCKER_CONFIG=/tmp/docker-nocreds docker pull …` — completes in seconds. `docker ps`/`exec`/`run` (with image present) work normally.

2. **Biome gate (ultracite v7 extends paths): fixed per-branch, not repo-wide.** biome.jsonc must extend `ultracite/biome/*` (v7 layout), not the v5-era `ultracite/core|react|next`; check/fix scripts must run the local ultracite pin, never `@latest`. Applied on Kheirah/agent-knowledge-hub-design (484e1a0 + 26327a7, 2026-07-11) and independently re-derived on Kheirah/continue-prev-task (fe73b90, 2026-07-12) — branches cut before those commits will still show "Could not resolve ultracite/core"; apply the same two-line fix. Repo-wide pre-existing findings remain (hundreds; scoped `bunx biome check <path>` is the usable gate for new work). The masterclass exhibit dir is mechanically clean as of fe73b90 (~36 judgment-rule findings left: noJsxPropsBind, noExportedImports, index keys).
   **Zombie dirty files:** entire.io (manual-commit strategy) snapshots uncommitted changes to a shadow branch and re-applies them post-commit ("carried forward remaining files") — a plain `git checkout --` of unwanted noise gets silently undone at the next commit. Cure: `git checkout -- <files> && entire clean --force` (drops the HEAD shadow branch + session carry-forward state; committed checkpoint history is unaffected).
   Also: Biome's `useSortedKeys` assist auto-sorts object keys on `--write` — it silently reorders semantically-ordered literals (MongoDB compound-index key specs). Guard such files with `// biome-ignore-all assist/source/useSortedKeys: …`.

3. **Vercel:** hasToggle.dev deploys as project `has-toggle-dev-web` under team scope `spiritsdontfly` (not the default `kheirahs-projects`, not `forsuxess`). Use `vercel ls/inspect --scope spiritsdontfly`; `vercel inspect --logs <url>` pulls build logs without switching scope. (2026-07-24)

4. **Bun override staleness:** after adding a root `overrides` entry, plain `bun install` updates `bun.lock` but can leave stale `.bun` store symlinks (nested dep still resolving to the old version). `rm -rf node_modules && bun install` is required for the override to actually take effect. (2026-07-24, radix-slot pin)

5. **The `web` app's locale-prefixed URLs 500 in dev.** `http://localhost:3001/en/learn/...` dies in middleware (`[NEMO] Middleware execution failed`); the unprefixed `http://localhost:3001/learn/...` serves fine. Use the unprefixed path when driving the site in a browser or the masterclass page looks broken when it isn't. `curl` also 500s on both (the middleware chain needs real browser headers) — verify with Playwright/Chrome DevTools, not curl. Next 16 also refuses to start a second dev server for the same project dir ("Run kill <pid> to stop it"), so reuse Eric's running server on 3001 rather than starting your own. (2026-07-25)

6. **Shared `.next` dir: `next build` then `next dev` corrupts some routes.** Running dev after a prod build in the same `apps/web/.next` produces `SyntaxError: Unexpected non-whitespace character after JSON` and 500s on a subset of routes (hit the nuqs-using learn pages, 2026-07-31, Next 16.2 + cacheComponents) while others serve fine. Cure: `rm -rf apps/web/.next` before starting dev. Don't misread the 500s as an app bug — the prod build of the same source passes.

7. **`vercel link` writes into `apps/web/.env.local` — never `rm` that file.** The CLI appends a `VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN` and reports "✓ Updated .env.local", so the file looks like a linking artifact when it is actually Eric's pre-existing local env (2846 bytes, gitignored, unrecoverable from git). A subagent ran `rm -rf .vercel .env.local` as "cleanup" and destroyed it (2026-08-10).
   **How to apply:** clean up after `vercel link` with `rm -rf apps/web/.vercel` only. If the env file is already gone, restore it from the source repo — `cp -p /Users/eric/Projects/hasToggle/hasToggle.dev/apps/web/.env.local apps/web/` — which is where Conductor seeds workspace copies from; the OIDC token is ephemeral and regenerates. Tell agents driving Vercel not to touch `.env.local` at all.

8. **Preview deploys are SSO-protected**, so `curl`/Playwright get an auth wall. Vercel's Protection Bypass for Automation is the documented way through — but it mints secrets that must be revoked afterwards, so verify revocation in the dashboard rather than trusting an agent's report. (2026-08-10)

9. **Cache-invalidation behaviour does not reproduce in `next dev`.** `updateTag` in dev goes through a tiered cache handler (built-in front handler paired with the real one, `server/use-cache/handlers.js`), so a `use cache` entry written during a server action survives a reload — on Vercel it does not, because the tag's expiry watermark is stamped after the render that wrote it. Anything testing `use cache` / `updateTag` / revalidation semantics must be verified on a preview deploy; a clean dev run proves nothing. (2026-08-10, landing-page shell demo)

10. **React DevTools extension throws spurious console errors on the rebake demo.** "The children should not have changed if we pass in the same set." with a stack entirely inside `chrome-extension://…/installHook.js` — the extension's fiber-mirror desyncs on transition commits with RSC children props + keyed remounts. Not an app bug: absent in extension-free browsers, string doesn't exist in React/Next/Radix bundles. Diagnose via `apps/web/.next/dev/logs/next-development.log` (timestamps are server *uptime*, not wall clock). (2026-08-19)

11. **`bun test` is not the full gate — it does not typecheck.** Vercel's build runs `bun run typecheck` (tsc) per workspace and fails on what bun test happily passes (e.g. a state-type gaining a required field while test literals lag: broke the build 2026-08-20). Before pushing any type-shape change: `cd apps/web && bun test && bun run typecheck`.

12. **Run `bun test` from inside the workspace dir, never the repo root.** Root `bun test` sweeps up every workspace's tests without their per-workspace `bunfig.toml` preloads, so `apps/web`'s fetch mocks are missing (`undefined is not an object (evaluating 'response.ok')` in email-validation tests) and mongodb throws an unhandled v8-snapshot error. The false failures look like regressions in files you never touched, and the test/file counts jump (189/30 → 208/34 was the tell, 2026-08-19). The usable gates: `cd apps/web && bun test`, or `turbo test --filter=web`.

13. **Lighthouse's default (simulated/Lantern) throttling is meaningless against `localhost`.** Because a local server has ~0 latency, every resource finishes inside the observed paint, so Lantern's pessimistic LCP graph charges LCP for the page's *entire* byte weight — LCP reads ~5s while the observed value is ~90ms and `observedFCP === observedLCP`. The number barely moves no matter what you cut (removing a 1.9s streaming hold, or all of Sentry, each shifted it <0.5s). Always add `--throttling-method=devtools` (real throttling) when benchmarking a local `next start`; on the landing page that was the difference between 80 and 100. Confirmed by the observed-vs-simulated fields in `audits.metrics.details.items[0]`. (2026-08-20)

14. **Fade-in entrance animations defer LCP by their full delay+duration.** An element animating `opacity: 0 → 1` is not a paint the browser counts, so LCP lands at `FCP + delay + duration` — the hero's `ht-enter` (80ms + 700ms) put LCP exactly 780ms after FCP in every run. Animating `transform` only, at full opacity (`ht-enter-opaque`/`ht-slide` in `apps/web/app/styles.css`), keeps the motion and makes the paint count immediately. Check this before blaming bundle size. (2026-08-20)

15. **Tailwind `scroll-smooth` on `<html>` needs `data-scroll-behavior="smooth"` beside it (Next 16).** The router's `disableSmoothScrollDuringRouteTransition` only suppresses CSS smooth scrolling during route-transition scroll resets when the html element carries the data attribute — it won't pay `getComputedStyle` to detect the CSS, and in production there's no warning. Without it every client-side navigation animates its scroll-to-top from the old position (~900ms of the new page sliding up); hash/anchor scrolls are exempt either way, so the glide survives the fix. Bit the lab pages 2026-08-21 (invisible before — the landing page had only anchor scrolls); fixed in `apps/web/app/layout.tsx` on Kheirah/playground-site-design.

# hasToggle.dev

**The unofficial live playground for Next.js and Vercel.**

Every chapter opens on something developers say — *"I'll put `use client` on it,
to be safe"*, *"It's either cached or it isn't"* — and runs the real feature next
to it. Not a screenshot of the feature, not a sandbox running a copy: the page
you are reading is the thing being demonstrated. Press the button, watch the
cache expire, open the drawer and read the code that did it.

The site is live at [hasToggle.dev](https://hastoggle.dev). This repo is the
whole of it, and [a second repo](https://github.com/hasToggle/hasToggle.dev-checkpoints)
publishes every prompt and checkpoint that produced it.

Not affiliated with Vercel. Nobody on the Next.js team sees a chapter before it
ships, which is where both the mistakes and the freedom come from.

---

## What's here

The playground has a book shape. `/lab` is the contents page; each chapter owns
a route segment at `/lab/<slug>`, so topics that are *made of* routes — parallel
routes, `not-found`, dynamic params, view transitions — can exist at all. A new
chapter lands every Monday, and the write-up goes out to the digest list the
same day.

| Chapter | Topic | Route |
|---|---|---|
| I'll put "use client" on it, to be safe. | server & client components | [`/lab/boundary`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/boundary) |
| I don't need state for a simple counter. | useState & re-renders | [`/lab/state`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/state) |
| It's either cached or it isn't. | caching & revalidation | [`/lab/caching`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/caching) |
| I'll fetch it all first, then render. | streaming & suspense | [`/lab/streaming`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/streaming) |
| You need an API route for that. | server actions & cookies | [`/lab/server-actions`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/server-actions) |
| I'll need to design a card for every page. | ImageResponse & route handlers | [`/lab/og-images`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/og-images) |

That table is a snapshot. `apps/web/app/[locale]/lab/syllabus.ts` is the source
of truth — read it there for what has shipped, what lands next Monday, and the
twenty-odd topics still queued.

The playground is free, permanently. The paid thing is coaching: small cohorts
building production apps on exactly these topics. The site doesn't get better if
you buy the cohort; it's the same page either way.

## Where the interesting code is

Most of this repo is infrastructure inherited from a template. The part that is
actually hasToggle is `apps/web`:

```
apps/web/app/[locale]/
├── (playground)/          one folder per chapter — the instruments
│   ├── boundary/          server vs client, rendered side by side
│   ├── shell/             the page re-baking itself (chapter: caching)
│   ├── stream/            three rows resolving in delay order
│   ├── mutation/          a form wired to a Server Action, no API route
│   ├── image/             /api/og drawing a card from a title
│   ├── state/             useState, replayed in slow motion
│   ├── navigation/        next up — the reading only, for now
│   └── demo-section.tsx   the editorial wrapper every chapter wears
├── lab/
│   ├── syllabus.ts        the registry that drives everything
│   ├── chapter.tsx        the shared chapter frame
│   └── <slug>/page.tsx    one page per chapter
└── components/            hero, contents bar, digest, FAQ, footer
```

Two things worth knowing before reading any of it:

**One registry, one source of truth.** `syllabus.ts` drives the contents rows,
the landing roadmap, the contents bar, the page-turn links, the sitemap, the OG
titles and the `/latest` redirect. Shipping a chapter is one entry flip —
`planned` → `next` → `shipped`, belief and nav label added — and nothing else to
keep in sync.

**Each chapter folder is self-contained.** `demo.tsx` (the instrument),
`source.ts` (the code the reference drawer shows), `index-value.tsx` (one true
reading from the running instrument, displayed on the contents row), and
whatever server actions and pure functions the chapter needs, with their tests
beside them.

## Running it

```sh
bun install
turbo dev --filter=web        # http://localhost:3001
```

`apps/web/env.ts` validates the environment through `@t3-oss/env-nextjs`. The
ones without which nothing starts: `NEXT_PUBLIC_WEB_URL`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL`,
`MONGODB_URI`, and the three `RESEND_*` keys the digest signup needs.

The gates, run from inside the workspace — not the repo root, which sweeps up
every workspace's tests without their per-workspace preloads and fails on files
you never touched:

```sh
cd apps/web
bun test
bun run typecheck             # bun test does not typecheck; the build gate does
```

**`next dev` lies about cache semantics.** A `use cache` entry written during a
Server Action survives a reload locally and does not on Vercel, because dev pairs
the real cache handler with a built-in front one. Anything touching `use cache`,
`updateTag` or revalidation has to be verified on a preview deploy; a clean dev
run proves nothing.

The other apps (`app`, `api`, `email`, `storybook`) come from the template and
are not part of the site. `apps/studio` is a stale Prisma Studio wrapper, dead
since the MongoDB migration.

## How it's built

In public, with AI. The work happens in [Conductor](https://conductor.build)
orchestrating Claude Code; [Entire.io](https://entire.io) publishes the process —
prompts, checkpoints, wrong turns included — to the checkpoints repo, and every
chapter page links the commits behind it. The AI writes the code. Someone still
has to decide what ships, and that part hasn't been automated.

Three documents govern the work, and they are worth reading before changing
anything a visitor sees:

- **`CLAUDE.md`** — repo conventions, commands, architecture. What an agent
  reads first.
- **`docs/voice.md`** — the writing voice for anything a visitor reads. Four
  registers, one stance, and an append-only record of lines that were rejected
  and why. It is short on purpose.
- **`docs/design.md`** — the instrument grammar every demo sits in: the state
  gauge, the view controls, the specimen, the deck, the reference bar. Plus the
  feedback rules and the verification traps.

Both docs update on a novel rejection, never on a schedule. A line that gets cut
because an existing rule predicted it means the guide worked and needs no edit.

CI is the Vercel deploy of `apps/web` plus Claude review actions; there is no
GitHub Actions test run. `turbo build` depends on `test` and `typecheck`, so the
deploy is the gate.

## Where this is going

### 1. The full range

The syllabus is everything Next.js can do, plus as much of Vercel as can be
proved from inside a web page. Six chapters are running; the rest still wear a
`+` — routing in all its forms, the asset pipeline, metadata and SEO, optimistic
UI, ISR, the edge network, feature flags, cron, storage, instant rollback. The
milestone is the Monday the `+` rows run out.

One chapter a week, in whatever order the work happens. There is no chapter
numbering anywhere on the site, because a number would only ever have recorded
which week the work got done.

### 2. The shop

A production application that is meta about its own implementation: a real (if
fictional) ecommerce site carrying a table of contents per page and per section,
listing every mechanism that page is made of. Click any piece of content and the
site shows you what's underneath it — which cache holds it, which boundary it
crossed, which route rendered it, which request it waited on.

The reason this is a separate milestone rather than more chapters: **a production
site is where features interact, and interaction is the one thing an isolated
demo cannot show.** A chapter can prove that a `use cache` entry refills when its
tag is deleted. It cannot show you what that looks like behind an intercepted
route, under a Server Action that also writes a cookie, on a page whose OG image
is generated from the same data that the cart is reading. The shop is where the
chapters meet each other, and where the answer to "how do I actually assemble
this" stops being left as an exercise.

Open questions, all of them real design work: what the surface is called and
where it lives; whether the inspector overlay can be built without breaking the
fixed instrument grammar the lab runs on; and whether a page's mechanism list is
authored or derived from the modules the page actually renders. The lab's whole
discipline is that one registry drives every list, and a hand-maintained
mechanism list would be the first thing on this site that could silently go
stale.

## Inherited from next-forge

The monorepo is a fork of [next-forge](https://github.com/vercel/next-forge), and
its bones are still load-bearing: the Turborepo layout, the `packages/*` split,
Biome via ultracite, the design system. What has diverged: the database is
MongoDB through the official driver with no ORM and no migrations, auth is
better-auth, and `apps/web` has been replaced entirely.

Bun workspaces, Turborepo, Next.js 16 with Cache Components, React 19,
TypeScript 7 (native), Tailwind 4, Bun's test runner.

## License

next-forge is MIT. This repo carries no license file of its own yet, so the code
written for hasToggle is public to read and not yet licensed for reuse.

orchestrating Claude Code; [Entire.io](https://entire.io) publishes the process —
prompts, checkpoints, wrong turns included — to the checkpoints repo, and every
chapter page links the commits behind it. The AI writes the code. Someone still
has to decide what ships, and that part hasn't been automated.

Three documents govern the work, and they are worth reading before changing
anything a visitor sees:

- **`CLAUDE.md`** — repo conventions, commands, architecture. What an agent
  reads first.
- **`docs/voice.md`** — the writing voice for anything a visitor reads. Four
  registers, one stance, and an append-only record of lines that were rejected
  and why. It is short on purpose.
- **`docs/design.md`** — the instrument grammar every demo sits in: the state
  gauge, the view controls, the specimen, the deck, the reference bar. Plus the
  feedback rules and the verification traps.

Both docs update on a novel rejection, never on a schedule. A line that gets cut
because an existing rule predicted it means the guide worked and needs no edit.

CI is the Vercel deploy of `apps/web` plus Claude review actions; there is no
GitHub Actions test run. `turbo build` depends on `test` and `typecheck`, so the
deploy is the gate.

## Where this is going

### 1. The full range

The syllabus is everything Next.js can do, plus as much of Vercel as can be
proved from inside a web page. Six chapters are running; the rest still wear a
`+` — routing in all its forms, the asset pipeline, metadata and SEO, optimistic
UI, ISR, the edge network, feature flags, cron, storage, instant rollback. The
milestone is the Monday the `+` rows run out.

One chapter a week, in whatever order the work happens. There is no chapter
numbering anywhere on the site, because a number would only ever have recorded
which week the work got done.

### 2. The shop

A production application that is meta about its own implementation: a real (if
fictional) ecommerce site carrying a table of contents per page and per section,
listing every mechanism that page is made of. Click any piece of content and the
site shows you what's underneath it — which cache holds it, which boundary it
crossed, which route rendered it, which request it waited on.

The reason this is a separate milestone rather than more chapters: **a production
site is where features interact, and interaction is the one thing an isolated
demo cannot show.** A chapter can prove that a `use cache` entry refills when its
tag is deleted. It cannot show you what that looks like behind an intercepted
route, under a Server Action that also writes a cookie, on a page whose OG image
is generated from the same data that the cart is reading. The shop is where the
chapters meet each other, and where the answer to "how do I actually assemble
this" stops being left as an exercise.

Open questions, all of them real design work: what the surface is called and
where it lives; whether the inspector overlay can be built without breaking the
fixed instrument grammar the lab runs on; and whether a page's mechanism list is
authored or derived from the modules the page actually renders. The lab's whole
discipline is that one registry drives every list, and a hand-maintained
mechanism list would be the first thing on this site that could silently go
stale.

## Inherited from next-forge

The monorepo is a fork of [next-forge](https://github.com/vercel/next-forge), and
its bones are still load-bearing: the Turborepo layout, the `packages/*` split,
Biome via ultracite, the design system. What has diverged: the database is
MongoDB through the official driver with no ORM and no migrations, auth is
better-auth, and `apps/web` has been replaced entirely.

Bun workspaces, Turborepo, Next.js 16 with Cache Components, React 19,
TypeScript 7 (native), Tailwind 4, Bun's test runner.

## License

next-forge is MIT. This repo carries no license file of its own yet, so the code
written for hasToggle is public to read and not yet licensed for reuse.

# hasToggle.dev

**The unofficial live playground for Next.js and Vercel.**

Every chapter opens on something developers say — *"I'll put `use client` on it,
to be safe"*, *"It's either cached or it isn't"* — and runs the real feature next
to it. Not a screenshot of the feature, not a sandbox running a copy: the page
you are reading is the thing being demonstrated. Press the button, watch the
cache expire, open the drawer and read the code that did it.

The site is live at [hasToggle.dev](https://hastoggle.dev). This repo is the
whole of it, and [a second repo](https://github.com/hasToggle/hasToggle.dev-checkpoints)
publishes every prompt and checkpoint that produced it.

Not affiliated with Vercel. Nobody on the Next.js team sees a chapter before it
ships, which is where both the mistakes and the freedom come from.

---

## What's here

The playground has a book shape. `/lab` is the contents page; each chapter owns
a route segment at `/lab/<slug>`, so topics that are *made of* routes — parallel
routes, `not-found`, dynamic params, view transitions — can exist at all. A new
chapter lands every Monday, and the write-up goes out to the digest list the
same day.

| Chapter | Topic | Route |
|---|---|---|
| I'll put "use client" on it, to be safe. | server & client components | [`/lab/boundary`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/boundary) |
| I don't need state for a simple counter. | useState & re-renders | [`/lab/state`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/state) |
| It's either cached or it isn't. | caching & revalidation | [`/lab/caching`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/caching) |
| I'll fetch it all first, then render. | streaming & suspense | [`/lab/streaming`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/streaming) |
| You need an API route for that. | server actions & cookies | [`/lab/server-actions`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/server-actions) |
| I'll need to design a card for every page. | ImageResponse & route handlers | [`/lab/og-images`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/og-images) |

That table is a snapshot. `apps/web/app/[locale]/lab/syllabus.ts` is the source
of truth — read it there for what has shipped, what lands next Monday, and the
twenty-odd topics still queued.

The playground is free, permanently. The paid thing is coaching: small cohorts
building production apps on exactly these topics. The site doesn't get better if
you buy the cohort; it's the same page either way.

## Where the interesting code is

Most of this repo is infrastructure inherited from a template. The part that is
actually hasToggle is `apps/web`:

```
apps/web/app/[locale]/
├── (playground)/          one folder per chapter — the instruments
│   ├── boundary/          server vs client, rendered side by side
│   ├── shell/             the page re-baking itself (chapter: caching)
│   ├── stream/            three rows resolving in delay order
│   ├── mutation/          a form wired to a Server Action, no API route
│   ├── image/             /api/og drawing a card from a title
│   ├── state/             useState, replayed in slow motion
│   ├── navigation/        next up — the reading only, for now
│   └── demo-section.tsx   the editorial wrapper every chapter wears
├── lab/
│   ├── syllabus.ts        the registry that drives everything
│   ├── chapter.tsx        the shared chapter frame
│   └── <slug>/page.tsx    one page per chapter
└── components/            hero, contents bar, digest, FAQ, footer
```

Two things worth knowing before reading any of it:

**One registry, one source of truth.** `syllabus.ts` drives the contents rows,
the landing roadmap, the contents bar, the page-turn links, the sitemap, the OG
titles and the `/latest` redirect. Shipping a chapter is one entry flip —
`planned` → `next` → `shipped`, belief and nav label added — and nothing else to
keep in sync.

**Each chapter folder is self-contained.** `demo.tsx` (the instrument),
`source.ts` (the code the reference drawer shows), `index-value.tsx` (one true
reading from the running instrument, displayed on the contents row), and
whatever server actions and pure functions the chapter needs, with their tests
beside them.

## Running it

```sh
bun install
turbo dev --filter=web        # http://localhost:3001
```

`apps/web/env.ts` validates the environment through `@t3-oss/env-nextjs`. The
ones without which nothing starts: `NEXT_PUBLIC_WEB_URL`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL`,
`MONGODB_URI`, and the three `RESEND_*` keys the digest signup needs.

The gates, run from inside the workspace — not the repo root, which sweeps up
every workspace's tests without their per-workspace preloads and fails on files
you never touched:

```sh
cd apps/web
bun test
bun run typecheck             # bun test does not typecheck; the build gate does
```

**`next dev` lies about cache semantics.** A `use cache` entry written during a
Server Action survives a reload locally and does not on Vercel, because dev pairs
the real cache handler with a built-in front one. Anything touching `use cache`,
`updateTag` or revalidation has to be verified on a preview deploy; a clean dev
run proves nothing.

The other apps (`app`, `api`, `email`, `storybook`) come from the template and
are not part of the site. `apps/studio` is a stale Prisma Studio wrapper, dead
since the MongoDB migration.

## How it's built

In public, with AI. The work happens in [Conductor](https://conductor.build)
orchestrating Claude Code; [Entire.io](https://entire.io) publishes the process —
prompts, checkpoints, wrong turns included — to the checkpoints repo, and every
chapter page links the commits behind it. The AI writes the code. Someone still
has to decide what ships, and that part hasn't been automated.

Three documents govern the work, and they are worth reading before changing
anything a visitor sees:

- **`CLAUDE.md`** — repo conventions, commands, architecture. What an agent
  reads first.
- **`docs/voice.md`** — the writing voice for anything a visitor reads. Four
  registers, one stance, and an append-only record of lines that were rejected
  and why. It is short on purpose.
- **`docs/design.md`** — the instrument grammar every demo sits in: the state
  gauge, the view controls, the specimen, the deck, the reference bar. Plus the
  feedback rules and the verification traps.

Both docs update on a novel rejection, never on a schedule. A line that gets cut
because an existing rule predicted it means the guide worked and needs no edit.

CI is the Vercel deploy of `apps/web` plus Claude review actions; there is no
GitHub Actions test run. `turbo build` depends on `test` and `typecheck`, so the
deploy is the gate.

## Where this is going

### 1. The full range

The syllabus is everything Next.js can do, plus as much of Vercel as can be
proved from inside a web page. Six chapters are running; the rest still wear a
`+` — routing in all its forms, the asset pipeline, metadata and SEO, optimistic
UI, ISR, the edge network, feature flags, cron, storage, instant rollback. The
milestone is the Monday the `+` rows run out.

One chapter a week, in whatever order the work happens. There is no chapter
numbering anywhere on the site, because a number would only ever have recorded
which week the work got done.

### 2. The shop

A production application that is meta about its own implementation: a real (if
fictional) ecommerce site carrying a table of contents per page and per section,
listing every mechanism that page is made of. Click any piece of content and the
site shows you what's underneath it — which cache holds it, which boundary it
crossed, which route rendered it, which request it waited on.

The reason this is a separate milestone rather than more chapters: **a production
site is where features interact, and interaction is the one thing an isolated
demo cannot show.** A chapter can prove that a `use cache` entry refills when its
tag is deleted. It cannot show you what that looks like behind an intercepted
route, under a Server Action that also writes a cookie, on a page whose OG image
is generated from the same data that the cart is reading. The shop is where the
chapters meet each other, and where the answer to "how do I actually assemble
this" stops being left as an exercise.

Open questions, all of them real design work: what the surface is called and
where it lives; whether the inspector overlay can be built without breaking the
fixed instrument grammar the lab runs on; and whether a page's mechanism list is
authored or derived from the modules the page actually renders. The lab's whole
discipline is that one registry drives every list, and a hand-maintained
mechanism list would be the first thing on this site that could silently go
stale.

## Inherited from next-forge

The monorepo is a fork of [next-forge](https://github.com/vercel/next-forge), and
its bones are still load-bearing: the Turborepo layout, the `packages/*` split,
Biome via ultracite, the design system. What has diverged: the database is
MongoDB through the official driver with no ORM and no migrations, auth is
better-auth, and `apps/web` has been replaced entirely.

Bun workspaces, Turborepo, Next.js 16 with Cache Components, React 19,
TypeScript 7 (native), Tailwind 4, Bun's test runner.

## License

next-forge is MIT. This repo carries no license file of its own yet, so the code
written for hasToggle is public to read and not yet licensed for reuse.

# hasToggle.dev

**The unofficial live playground for Next.js and Vercel.**

Every chapter opens on something developers say — *“I’ll put `use client` on it,
to be safe”*, *“It’s either cached or it isn’t”* — and runs the real feature next
to it. Not a screenshot of the feature, not a sandbox running a copy: the page
you are reading is the thing being demonstrated. Press the button, watch the
cache expire, open the drawer and read the code that did it.

The site is live at [hasToggle.dev](https://hastoggle.dev). This repo is the
whole of it, and [a second repo](https://github.com/hasToggle/hasToggle.dev-checkpoints)
publishes every prompt and checkpoint that produced it.

Not affiliated with Vercel. Nobody on the Next.js team sees a chapter before it
ships, which is where both the mistakes and the freedom come from.

---

## What’s here

The playground has a book shape. `/lab` is the contents page; each chapter owns
a route segment at `/lab/<slug>`, so topics that are *made of* routes — parallel
routes, `not-found`, dynamic params, view transitions — can exist at all. A new
chapter lands every Monday, and the write-up goes out to the digest list the
same day.

| Chapter | Topic | Route |
|---|---|---|
| I’ll put “use client” on it, to be safe. | server & client components | [`/lab/boundary`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/boundary) |
| I don’t need state for a simple counter. | useState & re-renders | [`/lab/state`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/state) |
| It’s either cached or it isn’t. | caching & revalidation | [`/lab/caching`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/caching) |
| I’ll fetch it all first, then render. | streaming & suspense | [`/lab/streaming`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/streaming) |
| You need an API route for that. | server actions & cookies | [`/lab/server-actions`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/server-actions) |
| I’ll need to design a card for every page. | ImageResponse & route handlers | [`/lab/og-images`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/og-images) |

That table is a snapshot. `apps/web/app/[locale]/lab/syllabus.ts` is the source
of truth — read it there for what has shipped, what lands next Monday, and the
twenty-odd topics still queued.

The playground is free, permanently. The paid thing is coaching: small cohorts
building production apps on exactly these topics. The site doesn’t get better if
you buy the cohort; it’s the same page either way.

## Where the interesting code is

Most of this repo is infrastructure inherited from a template. The part that is
actually hasToggle is `apps/web`:

```
apps/web/app/[locale]/
├── (playground)/          one folder per chapter — the instruments
│   ├── boundary/          server vs client, rendered side by side
│   ├── shell/             the page re-baking itself (chapter: caching)
│   ├── stream/            three rows resolving in delay order
│   ├── mutation/          a form wired to a Server Action, no API route
│   ├── image/             /api/og drawing a card from a title
│   ├── state/             useState, replayed in slow motion
│   ├── navigation/        next up — the reading only, for now
│   └── demo-section.tsx   the editorial wrapper every chapter wears
├── lab/
│   ├── syllabus.ts        the registry that drives everything
│   ├── chapter.tsx        the shared chapter frame
│   └── <slug>/page.tsx    one page per chapter
└── components/            hero, contents bar, digest, FAQ, footer
```

Two things worth knowing before reading any of it:

**One registry, one source of truth.** `syllabus.ts` drives the contents rows,
the landing roadmap, the contents bar, the page-turn links, the sitemap, the OG
titles and the `/latest` redirect. Shipping a chapter is one entry flip —
`planned` → `next` → `shipped`, belief and nav label added — and nothing else to
keep in sync.

**Each chapter folder is self-contained.** `demo.tsx` (the instrument),
`source.ts` (the code the reference drawer shows), `index-value.tsx` (one true
reading from the running instrument, displayed on the contents row), and
whatever server actions and pure functions the chapter needs, with their tests
beside them.

## Running it

```sh
bun install
turbo dev --filter=web        # http://localhost:3001
```

`apps/web/env.ts` validates the environment through `@t3-oss/env-nextjs`. The
ones without which nothing starts: `NEXT_PUBLIC_WEB_URL`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL`,
`MONGODB_URI`, and the three `RESEND_*` keys the digest signup needs.

The gates, run from inside the workspace — not the repo root, which sweeps up
every workspace’s tests without their per-workspace preloads and fails on files
you never touched:

```sh
cd apps/web
bun test
bun run typecheck             # bun test does not typecheck; the build gate does
```

**`next dev` lies about cache semantics.** A `use cache` entry written during a
Server Action survives a reload locally and does not on Vercel, because dev pairs
the real cache handler with a built-in front one. Anything touching `use cache`,
`updateTag` or revalidation has to be verified on a preview deploy; a clean dev
run proves nothing.

The other apps (`app`, `api`, `email`, `storybook`) come from the template and
are not part of the site. `apps/studio` is a stale Prisma Studio wrapper, dead
since the MongoDB migration.

## How it’s built

In public, with AI. The work happens in Conductor orchestrating Claude Code, and
Entire.io publishes the process — prompts, checkpoints, wrong turns included — to
the checkpoints repo, with every chapter page linking the commits behind it. The AI writes the code. Someone still
has to decide what ships, and that part hasn’t been automated.

Three documents govern the work, and they are worth reading before changing
anything a visitor sees:

- **`CLAUDE.md`** — repo conventions, commands, architecture. What an agent
  reads first.
- **`docs/voice.md`** — the writing voice for anything a visitor reads. Four
  registers, one stance, and an append-only record of lines that were rejected
  and why. It is short on purpose.
- **`docs/design.md`** — the instrument grammar every demo sits in: the state
  gauge, the view controls, the specimen, the deck, the reference bar. Plus the
  feedback rules and the verification traps.

Both docs update on a novel rejection, never on a schedule. A line that gets cut
because an existing rule predicted it means the guide worked and needs no edit.

CI is the Vercel deploy of `apps/web` plus Claude review actions; there is no
GitHub Actions test run. `turbo build` depends on `test` and `typecheck`, so the
deploy is the gate.

## Where this is going

### 1. The full range

The syllabus is everything Next.js can do, plus as much of Vercel as can be
proved from inside a web page. Six chapters are running; the rest still wear a
`+` — routing in all its forms, the asset pipeline, metadata and SEO, optimistic
UI, ISR, the edge network, feature flags, cron, storage, instant rollback. The
milestone is the Monday the `+` rows run out.

One chapter a week, in whatever order the work happens. There is no chapter
numbering anywhere on the site, because a number would only ever have recorded
which week the work got done.

### 2. The shop

A production application that is meta about its own implementation: a real (if
fictional) ecommerce site carrying a table of contents per page and per section,
listing every mechanism that page is made of. Click any piece of content and the
site shows you what’s underneath it — which cache holds it, which boundary it
crossed, which route rendered it, which request it waited on.

The reason this is a separate milestone rather than more chapters: **a production
site is where features interact, and interaction is the one thing an isolated
demo cannot show.** A chapter can prove that a `use cache` entry refills when its
tag is deleted. It cannot show you what that looks like behind an intercepted
route, under a Server Action that also writes a cookie, on a page whose OG image
is generated from the same data that the cart is reading. The shop is where the
chapters meet each other, and where the answer to "how do I actually assemble
this" stops being left as an exercise.

Open questions, all of them real design work: what the surface is called and
where it lives; whether the inspector overlay can be built without breaking the
fixed instrument grammar the lab runs on; and whether a page’s mechanism list is
authored or derived from the modules the page actually renders. The lab’s whole
discipline is that one registry drives every list, and a hand-maintained
mechanism list would be the first thing on this site that could silently go
stale.

## Inherited from next-forge

The monorepo is a fork of [next-forge](https://github.com/vercel/next-forge), and
its bones are still load-bearing: the Turborepo layout, the `packages/*` split,
Biome via ultracite, the design system. What has diverged: the database is
MongoDB through the official driver with no ORM and no migrations, auth is
better-auth, and `apps/web` has been replaced entirely.

Bun workspaces, Turborepo, Next.js 16 with Cache Components, React 19,
TypeScript 7 (native), Tailwind 4, Bun’s test runner.

## License

next-forge is MIT. This repo carries no license file of its own yet, so the code
written for hasToggle is public to read and not yet licensed for reuse.
