# hasToggle.dev

**The unofficial live playground for Next.js and Vercel.**

Every chapter opens on something developers say — *“I’ll put `use client` on it,
to be safe”*, *“It’s either cached or it isn’t”* — and runs the real feature next
to it. Not a screenshot of the feature, not a sandbox running a copy: the page
you are reading is the thing being demonstrated. Press the button, watch the
cache expire, open the drawer and read the code that did it.

The site is live at [hasToggle.dev](https://hastoggle.dev). This repo is the
whole of it, and [a second repo](https://github.com/hasToggle/hasToggle.dev-checkpoints)
publishes every prompt and checkpoint that produced it.

Not affiliated with Vercel. Nobody on the Next.js team sees a chapter before it
ships, which is where both the mistakes and the freedom come from.

---

## What’s here

The playground has a book shape. `/lab` is the contents page; each chapter owns
a route segment at `/lab/<slug>`, so topics that are *made of* routes — parallel
routes, `not-found`, dynamic params, view transitions — can exist at all. A new
chapter lands every Monday, and the write-up goes out to the digest list the
same day.

| Chapter | Topic | Route |
|---|---|---|
| I’ll put “use client” on it, to be safe. | server & client components | [`/lab/boundary`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/boundary) |
| I don’t need state for a simple counter. | useState & re-renders | [`/lab/state`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/state) |
| It’s either cached or it isn’t. | caching & revalidation | [`/lab/caching`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/caching) |
| I’ll fetch it all first, then render. | streaming & suspense | [`/lab/streaming`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/streaming) |
| You need an API route for that. | server actions & cookies | [`/lab/server-actions`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/server-actions) |
| I’ll need to design a card for every page. | ImageResponse & route handlers | [`/lab/og-images`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/og-images) |

That table is a snapshot. `apps/web/app/[locale]/lab/syllabus.ts` is the source
of truth — read it there for what has shipped, what lands next Monday, and the
twenty-odd topics still queued.

The playground is free, permanently. The paid thing is coaching: small cohorts
building production apps on exactly these topics. The site doesn’t get better if
you buy the cohort; it’s the same page either way.

## Where the interesting code is

Most of this repo is infrastructure inherited from a template. The part that is
actually hasToggle is `apps/web`:

```
apps/web/app/[locale]/
├── (playground)/          one folder per chapter — the instruments
│   ├── boundary/          server vs client, rendered side by side
│   ├── shell/             the page re-baking itself (chapter: caching)
│   ├── stream/            three rows resolving in delay order
│   ├── mutation/          a form wired to a Server Action, no API route
│   ├── image/             /api/og drawing a card from a title
│   ├── state/             useState, replayed in slow motion
│   ├── navigation/        next up — the reading only, for now
│   └── demo-section.tsx   the editorial wrapper every chapter wears
├── lab/
│   ├── syllabus.ts        the registry that drives everything
│   ├── chapter.tsx        the shared chapter frame
│   └── <slug>/page.tsx    one page per chapter
└── components/            hero, contents bar, digest, FAQ, footer
```

Two things worth knowing before reading any of it:

**One registry, one source of truth.** `syllabus.ts` drives the contents rows,
the landing roadmap, the contents bar, the page-turn links, the sitemap, the OG
titles and the `/latest` redirect. Shipping a chapter is one entry flip —
`planned` → `next` → `shipped`, belief and nav label added — and nothing else to
keep in sync.

**Each chapter folder is self-contained.** `demo.tsx` (the instrument),
`source.ts` (the code the reference drawer shows), `index-value.tsx` (one true
reading from the running instrument, displayed on the contents row), and
whatever server actions and pure functions the chapter needs, with their tests
beside them.

## Running it

```sh
bun install
turbo dev --filter=web        # http://localhost:3001
```

`apps/web/env.ts` validates the environment through `@t3-oss/env-nextjs`. The
ones without which nothing starts: `NEXT_PUBLIC_WEB_URL`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL`,
`MONGODB_URI`, and the three `RESEND_*` keys the digest signup needs.

The gates, run from inside the workspace — not the repo root, which sweeps up
every workspace’s tests without their per-workspace preloads and fails on files
you never touched:

```sh
cd apps/web
bun test
bun run typecheck             # bun test does not typecheck; the build gate does
```

**`next dev` lies about cache semantics.** A `use cache` entry written during a
Server Action survives a reload locally and does not on Vercel, because dev pairs
the real cache handler with a built-in front one. Anything touching `use cache`,
`updateTag` or revalidation has to be verified on a preview deploy; a clean dev
run proves nothing.

The other apps (`app`, `api`, `email`, `storybook`) come from the template and
are not part of the site. `apps/studio` is a stale Prisma Studio wrapper, dead
since the MongoDB migration.

## How it’s built

In public, with AI. The work happens in Conductor orchestrating Claude Code, and
Entire.io publishes the process — prompts, checkpoints, wrong turns included — to
the checkpoints repo, with every chapter page linking the commits behind it. The
AI writes the code. Someone still has to decide what ships, and that part hasn’t
been automated.

Three documents govern the work, and they are worth reading before changing
anything a visitor sees:

- **`CLAUDE.md`** — repo conventions, commands, architecture. What an agent
  reads first.
- **`docs/voice.md`** — the writing voice for anything a visitor reads. Four
  registers, one stance, and an append-only record of lines that were rejected
  and why. It is short on purpose.
- **`docs/design.md`** — the instrument grammar every demo sits in: the state
  gauge, the view controls, the specimen, the deck, the reference bar. Plus the
  feedback rules and the verification traps.

Both docs update on a novel rejection, never on a schedule. A line that gets cut
because an existing rule predicted it means the guide worked and needs no edit.

CI is the Vercel deploy of `apps/web` plus Claude review actions; there is no
GitHub Actions test run. `turbo build` depends on `test` and `typecheck`, so the
deploy is the gate.

## Where this is going

### 1. The full range

The syllabus is everything Next.js can do, plus as much of Vercel as can be
proved from inside a web page. Six chapters are running; the rest still wear a
`+` — routing in all its forms, the asset pipeline, metadata and SEO, optimistic
UI, ISR, the edge network, feature flags, cron, storage, instant rollback. The
milestone is the Monday the `+` rows run out.

One chapter a week, in whatever order the work happens. There is no chapter
numbering anywhere on the site, because a number would only ever have recorded
which week the work got done.

### 2. The shop

A production application that is meta about its own implementation: a real (if
fictional) ecommerce site carrying a table of contents per page and per section,
listing every mechanism that page is made of. Click any piece of content and the
site shows you what’s underneath it — which cache holds it, which boundary it
crossed, which route rendered it, which request it waited on.

The reason this is a separate milestone rather than more chapters: **a production
site is where features interact, and interaction is the one thing an isolated
demo cannot show.** A chapter can prove that a `use cache` entry refills when its
tag is deleted. It cannot show you what that looks like behind an intercepted
route, under a Server Action that also writes a cookie, on a page whose OG image
is generated from the same data that the cart is reading. The shop is where the
chapters meet each other, and where the answer to "how do I actually assemble
this" stops being left as an exercise.

Open questions, all of them real design work: what the surface is called and
where it lives; whether the inspector overlay can be built without breaking the
fixed instrument grammar the lab runs on; and whether a page’s mechanism list is
authored or derived from the modules the page actually renders. The lab’s whole
discipline is that one registry drives every list, and a hand-maintained
mechanism list would be the first thing on this site that could silently go
stale.

## Inherited from next-forge

The monorepo is a fork of [next-forge](https://github.com/vercel/next-forge), and
its bones are still load-bearing: the Turborepo layout, the `packages/*` split,
Biome via ultracite, the design system. What has diverged: the database is
MongoDB through the official driver with no ORM and no migrations, auth is
better-auth, and `apps/web` has been replaced entirely.

Bun workspaces, Turborepo, Next.js 16 with Cache Components, React 19,
TypeScript 7 (native), Tailwind 4, Bun’s test runner.

## License

next-forge is MIT. This repo carries no license file of its own yet, so the code
written for hasToggle is public to read and not yet licensed for reuse.

# hasToggle.dev

**The unofficial live playground for Next.js and Vercel.**

Every chapter opens on something developers say — *“I’ll put `use client` on it,
to be safe”*, *“It’s either cached or it isn’t”* — and runs the real feature next
to it. Not a screenshot of the feature, not a sandbox running a copy: the page
you are reading is the thing being demonstrated. Press the button, watch the
cache expire, open the drawer and read the code that did it.

The site is live at [hasToggle.dev](https://hastoggle.dev). This repo is the
whole of it, and [a second repo](https://github.com/hasToggle/hasToggle.dev-checkpoints)
publishes every prompt and checkpoint that produced it.

Not affiliated with Vercel. Nobody on the Next.js team sees a chapter before it
ships, which is where both the mistakes and the freedom come from.

---

## What’s here

The playground has a book shape. `/lab` is the contents page; each chapter owns
a route segment at `/lab/<slug>`, so topics that are *made of* routes — parallel
routes, `not-found`, dynamic params, view transitions — can exist at all. A new
chapter lands every Monday, and the write-up goes out to the digest list the
same day.

| Chapter | Topic | Route |
|---|---|---|
| I’ll put “use client” on it, to be safe. | server & client components | [`/lab/boundary`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/boundary) |
| I don’t need state for a simple counter. | useState & re-renders | [`/lab/state`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/state) |
| It’s either cached or it isn’t. | caching & revalidation | [`/lab/caching`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/caching) |
| I’ll fetch it all first, then render. | streaming & suspense | [`/lab/streaming`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/streaming) |
| You need an API route for that. | server actions & cookies | [`/lab/server-actions`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/server-actions) |
| I’ll need to design a card for every page. | ImageResponse & route handlers | [`/lab/og-images`](https://hastoggle.dev/lab/og-images) |

That table is a snapshot. `apps/web/app/[locale]/lab/syllabus.ts` is the source
of truth — read it there for what has shipped, what lands next Monday, and the
twenty-odd topics still queued.

The playground is free, permanently. The paid thing is coaching: small cohorts
building production apps on exactly these topics. The site doesn’t get better if
you buy the cohort; it’s the same page either way.

## Where the interesting code is

Most of this repo is infrastructure inherited from a template. The part that is
actually hasToggle is `apps/web`:

```
apps/web/app/[locale]/
├── (playground)/          one folder per chapter — the instruments
│   ├── boundary/          server vs client, rendered side by side
│   ├── shell/             the page re-baking itself (chapter: caching)
│   ├── stream/            three rows resolving in delay order
│   ├── mutation/          a form wired to a Server Action, no API route
│   ├── image/             /api/og drawing a card from a title
│   ├── state/             useState, replayed in slow motion
│   ├── navigation/        next up — the reading only, for now
│   └── demo-section.tsx   the editorial wrapper every chapter wears
├── lab/
│   ├── syllabus.ts        the registry that drives everything
│   ├── chapter.tsx        the shared chapter frame
│   └── <slug>/page.tsx    one page per chapter
└── components/            hero, contents bar, digest, FAQ, footer
```

Two things worth knowing before reading any of it:

**One registry, one source of truth.** `syllabus.ts` drives the contents rows,
the landing roadmap, the contents bar, the page-turn links, the sitemap, the OG
titles and the `/latest` redirect. Shipping a chapter is one entry flip —
`planned` → `next` → `shipped`, belief and nav label added — and nothing else to
keep in sync.

**Each chapter folder is self-contained.** `demo.tsx` (the instrument),
`source.ts` (the code the reference drawer shows), `index-value.tsx` (one true
reading from the running instrument, displayed on the contents row), and
whatever server actions and pure functions the chapter needs, with their tests
beside them.

## Running it

```sh
bun install
turbo dev --filter=web        # http://localhost:3001
```

`apps/web/env.ts` validates the environment through `@t3-oss/env-nextjs`. The
ones without which nothing starts: `NEXT_PUBLIC_WEB_URL`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL`,
`MONGODB_URI`, and the three `RESEND_*` keys the digest signup needs.

The gates, run from inside the workspace — not the repo root, which sweeps up
every workspace’s tests without their per-workspace preloads and fails on files
you never touched:

```sh
cd apps/web
bun test
bun run typecheck             # bun test does not typecheck; the build gate does
```

**`next dev` lies about cache semantics.** A `use cache` entry written during a
Server Action survives a reload locally and does not on Vercel, because dev pairs
the real cache handler with a built-in front one. Anything touching `use cache`,
`updateTag` or revalidation has to be verified on a preview deploy; a clean dev
run proves nothing.

The other apps (`app`, `api`, `email`, `storybook`) come from the template and
are not part of the site. `apps/studio` is a stale Prisma Studio wrapper, dead
since the MongoDB migration.

## How it’s built

In public, with AI. The work happens in Conductor orchestrating Claude Code, and
Entire.io publishes the process — prompts, checkpoints, wrong turns included — to
the checkpoints repo, with every chapter page linking the commits behind it. The
AI writes the code. Someone still has to decide what ships, and that part hasn’t
been automated.

Three documents govern the work, and they are worth reading before changing
anything a visitor sees:

- **`CLAUDE.md`** — repo conventions, commands, architecture. What an agent
  reads first.
- **`docs/voice.md`** — the writing voice for anything a visitor reads. Four
  registers, one stance, and an append-only record of lines that were rejected
  and why. It is short on purpose.
- **`docs/design.md`** — the instrument grammar every demo sits in: the state
  gauge, the view controls, the specimen, the deck, the reference bar. Plus the
  feedback rules and the verification traps.

Both docs update on a novel rejection, never on a schedule. A line that gets cut
because an existing rule predicted it means the guide worked and needs no edit.

CI is the Vercel deploy of `apps/web` plus Claude review actions; there is no
GitHub Actions test run. `turbo build` depends on `test` and `typecheck`, so the
deploy is the gate.

## Where this is going

### 1. The full range

The syllabus is everything Next.js can do, plus as much of Vercel as can be
proved from inside a web page. Six chapters are running; the rest still wear a
`+` — routing in all its forms, the asset pipeline, metadata and SEO, optimistic
UI, ISR, the edge network, feature flags, cron, storage, instant rollback. The
milestone is the Monday the `+` rows run out.

One chapter a week, in whatever order the work happens. There is no chapter
numbering anywhere on the site, because a number would only ever have recorded
which week the work got done.

### 2. The shop

A production application that is meta about its own implementation: a real (if
fictional) ecommerce site carrying a table of contents per page and per section,
listing every mechanism that page is made of. Click any piece of content and the
site shows you what’s underneath it — which cache holds it, which boundary it
crossed, which route rendered it, which request it waited on.

The reason this is a separate milestone rather than more chapters: **a production
site is where features interact, and interaction is the one thing an isolated
demo cannot show.** A chapter can prove that a `use cache` entry refills when its
tag is deleted. It cannot show you what that looks like behind an intercepted
route, under a Server Action that also writes a cookie, on a page whose OG image
is generated from the same data that the cart is reading. The shop is where the
chapters meet each other, and where the answer to "how do I actually assemble
this" stops being left as an exercise.

Open questions, all of them real design work: what the surface is called and
where it lives; whether the inspector overlay can be built without breaking the
fixed instrument grammar the lab runs on; and whether a page’s mechanism list is
authored or derived from the modules the page actually renders. The lab’s whole
discipline is that one registry drives every list, and a hand-maintained
mechanism list would be the first thing on this site that could silently go
stale.

## Scaffolded from next-forge

The monorepo was generated by
[next-forge](https://github.com/vercel/next-forge) — `npx next-forge init`, which
copies the template and starts a fresh history. There is no upstream and no
shared commits, so nothing here gets pulled or updated from it; divergence is the
point.

Its bones are still load-bearing: the Turborepo layout, the `packages/*` split,
Biome via ultracite, the design system. What has diverged: the database is
MongoDB through the official driver with no ORM and no migrations, auth is
better-auth, and `apps/web` has been replaced entirely. A few pieces of the
template’s own repo furniture came along in the copy and never had a job here —
the `has-toggle` bin and its CLI dependencies, the issue and PR templates.

Bun workspaces, Turborepo, Next.js 16 with Cache Components, React 19,
TypeScript 7 (native), Tailwind 4, Bun’s test runner.

## License

next-forge is MIT. This repo carries no license file of its own yet, so the code
written for hasToggle is public to read and not yet licensed for reuse.

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Overview

This is a **has-toggle** monorepo - a production-grade Turborepo template for Next.js SaaS applications. The codebase is built around five core principles: Fast, Cheap, Opinionated, Modern, and Safe. It uses Bun workspaces and Turborepo for managing multiple applications and shared packages.

## Development Commands

### Setup & Installation
```bash
bun install                    # Install all dependencies
```

Set `MONGODB_URI` in the environment (validated via @t3-oss/env-nextjs in `packages/database/keys.ts`).

### Running Applications
```bash
bun dev                       # Run all apps in development mode
turbo dev --filter=app         # Run only the main app (port 3000)
turbo dev --filter=web         # Run only the web/marketing site (port 3001)
turbo dev --filter=api         # Run only the API (port 3002, includes Stripe webhook listener)
```

### Testing
```bash
bun test                      # Run tests across all workspaces
turbo test --filter=app        # Run tests for specific app
bun test                       # Run Bun test runner in apps/app or apps/api
```

### Code Quality
```bash
bun run check                     # Run Biome linter/formatter checks (uses ultracite presets)
bun run fix                       # Auto-fix linting/formatting issues
turbo boundaries               # Check package boundaries
```

### Building
```bash
bun run build                     # Build all apps (depends on tests passing)
turbo build --filter=app       # Build specific app
turbo analyze --filter=app     # Analyze bundle size
```

### Database

The database is MongoDB, accessed through the official `mongodb` driver — there is no ORM, no schema migrations, and no generated client. `packages/database/index.ts` exports a `database` object with typed collection handles; document types live in `packages/database/types.ts`.

### Maintenance
```bash
bun run bump-deps                 # Update dependencies (excludes recharts)
bun run bump-ui                   # Update shadcn/ui components
bun run clean                     # Clean node_modules from root
turbo clean                    # Clean build artifacts and node_modules from all workspaces
```

## Architecture

### Monorepo Structure

The repository uses **Bun workspaces** with two main directories:

- **apps/** - Deployable applications (independently deployable)
- **packages/** - Shared packages consumed by apps

### Applications (apps/)

1. **app** (port 3000) - Main SaaS application
   - Authentication via better-auth (route groups: `(authenticated)` and `(unauthenticated)`); handler mounted at `/api/auth/[...all]`
   - Uses Next.js 16 with App Router
   - Server actions in `app/actions/`
   - API routes in `app/api/`
   - Tests configured with Bun test runner

2. **web** (port 3001) - Marketing/landing page
   - Internationalization support (uses `[locale]` route)
   - Content management via CMS package
   - Rate limiting via Arcjet

3. **api** (port 3002) - RESTful API server
   - Health check endpoint at `/health`
   - Webhook handlers in `app/webhooks/`
   - Cron jobs in `app/cron/`
   - Development includes Stripe webhook listener (requires Stripe CLI)

4. **email** - Email templates (React Email)
5. **storybook** (`apps/storybook`) - Component development environment.
   Its package name is `@repo/storybook`, **not** `storybook`: Bun links every
   workspace package into the root `node_modules` by name, so a workspace named
   `storybook` shadows the real `storybook` npm package and every addon that
   imports `storybook/internal/*` fails to resolve. Turbo filter is
   `--filter=@repo/storybook`. Never name a workspace after one of its own
   dependencies.
6. **studio** - Database management UI (stale Prisma Studio wrapper; non-functional since the MongoDB migration)

### Shared Packages (packages/)

Core infrastructure packages:

- **@repo/auth** - better-auth authentication (client, server, middleware, provider)
  - MongoDB adapter + organization plugin; the active org id is the tenant id
  - Server instance in `instance.ts`; `server.ts` is a Clerk-shaped compat layer
    (`auth()`, `currentUser()`) so callers did not have to change
  - Handler mounted by apps/app at `/api/auth/[...all]`
- **@repo/database** - MongoDB via the official `mongodb` driver (server-only)
  - Typed collection handles exported from `packages/database/index.ts`
  - Document types at `packages/database/types.ts`
  - Requires `MONGODB_URI` (validated in `packages/database/keys.ts`)
- **@repo/design-system** - shadcn/ui component library
  - Components in `components/` (auto-generated, excluded from Biome linting)
  - Providers for themes, tooltips, etc.
  - Dark mode support via next-themes
- **@repo/observability** - Sentry error tracking and logging
- **@repo/security** - Arcjet integration for application security
- **@repo/analytics** - Google Analytics and PostHog
- **@repo/payments** - Stripe integration
- **@repo/email** - Resend email service
- **@repo/webhooks** - Webhook handling (inbound/outbound)
- **@repo/collaboration** - Real-time features (Liveblocks)
- **@repo/feature-flags** - Feature flag management
- **@repo/notifications** - In-app notifications
- **@repo/internationalization** - i18n support
- **@repo/cms** - Content management (BaseHub)
- **@repo/seo** - SEO utilities
- **@repo/storage** - File upload/management
- **@repo/ai** - AI integration utilities

### Technology Stack

- **Framework**: Next.js 16 with App Router, React 19
- **Language**: TypeScript 5.9 (strict mode, NodeNext module resolution)
- **Package Manager**: Bun 1.1.43
- **Build Tool**: Turborepo 2.5.8
- **Database**: MongoDB via the official `mongodb` driver 7.x
- **Auth**: better-auth (email/password + organizations)
- **Styling**: Tailwind CSS 4.1
- **Linting**: Biome 2.3.1 with ultracite presets (core, react, next)
- **Testing**: Bun test runner
- **Bundling**: tsup for package builds

### Important Patterns

1. **Workspace Dependencies**: Internal packages use `workspace:*` protocol
   - Example: `"@repo/auth": "workspace:*"`

2. **Route Groups**: Apps use Next.js route groups for layout separation
   - app: `(authenticated)` and `(unauthenticated)` groups
   - web: `[locale]` for internationalization

3. **Server/Client Separation**: Packages use `server-only` for server-side code
   - Database and auth server utilities are server-only
   - Client components/utilities are separate files

4. **Environment Variables**: Uses @t3-oss/env-nextjs for type-safe env validation

5. **Path Aliases**: Apps configure aliases via tsconfig.json paths
   - `@/` - points to app root
   - `@repo/` - points to packages directory

6. **Biome Exclusions**: Auto-generated code excluded from linting:
   - `packages/design-system/components/ui` (shadcn components)
   - `packages/collaboration/config.ts` (Liveblocks config)
   - `packages/cms/basehub-types.d.ts` (CMS types)

7. **Build Dependencies**: `turbo.json` configures build to depend on tests passing
   - Builds run `^build` (dependency builds) then `test` before building

## Key Files

- `turbo.json` - Turborepo task pipeline configuration
- `biome.jsonc` - Linter/formatter configuration (extends ultracite presets)
- `packages/database/types.ts` - Database document types
- `docs/voice.md` - The writing voice for anything a visitor reads
- `docs/design.md` - The instrument design grammar for the playground demos
- Root `package.json` - Monorepo scripts, workspace configuration, and CLI entry point (`dist/index.js`)

## Writing copy

Any user-facing prose in `apps/web` or `packages/email` — exhibit titles, demo
prose, asides, panel labels, FAQ answers, digest copy — follows `docs/voice.md`.
Read it before drafting, and edit against its three passes (§5) before calling
copy done. It is short on purpose; do not skim it.

Do not add rules to it casually. A rejected line that an existing rule already
predicted means the guide worked and needs no edit — see §9.

## Designing demos

Demo UI follows `docs/design.md` — the fixed instrument grammar (state gauge,
view controls, specimen, deck, reference bar), the feedback rules, and the
current migration state. Read it before building or reshaping an exhibit.
Copy and demo co-evolve: when a panel gains a capability, re-run voice.md's
three passes over the exhibit's prose, because the instrument may have
obsoleted lines that were accurate when they shipped.

Design rounds in this repo run on proposals: present options with a clear
recommendation and the trade-offs named, get an explicit yes, then build.
Project knowledge belongs in the repo — these docs, not external notes.

## Development Notes

- The main branch is not explicitly configured in git - PRs should target the default branch
- Apps have independent dev ports: app (3000), web (3001), api (3002)
- API development automatically runs Stripe CLI webhook forwarding to localhost:3002/webhooks/payments
- MongoDB access goes through the shared client in `packages/database/index.ts` (cached on `global` in development to survive hot reloads)
- Tests must pass before builds complete (enforced by Turborepo pipeline)
- The design system excludes shadcn auto-generated UI components from version control linting

<!-- NEXT-AGENTS-MD-START -->
[Next.js Docs]
STOP. What you remember about Next.js is WRONG for this project. Read the docs before any Next.js task.
The full, version-matched docs ship inside the installed package: `apps/web/node_modules/next/dist/docs/` — markdown mirroring nextjs.org/docs (`01-app/01-getting-started/`, `01-app/02-guides/`, `01-app/03-api-reference/`, `02-pages/`, `03-architecture/`). Search there with grep/glob; there is no `.next-docs` directory in this repo. The `nextjs_docs` MCP tool (next-devtools) returns this same path.
<!-- NEXT-AGENTS-MD-END -->

Done — pushed to `Kheirah/playground-site-design`, folded into PR #392 (now 51 commits).

**Verification first — and it caught one thing.** `scripts/skip-ci.js` is *not* dead: all four `apps/*/vercel.json` name it as their `ignoreCommand`. Deleting `scripts/` wholesale would have broken every app's Vercel Ignored Build Step. It stays; only the CLI files around it went.

**Removed, each confirmed unreferenced first:**

| Removed | Verified by |
|---|---|
| `scripts/{index,initialize,update,utils}.ts` | next-forge's own published CLI — `init` clones next-forge, `update` migrates between its versions. Self-contained import cluster; nothing else imports them |
| `tsup.config.ts` + `tsup` devDep | its only `entry` was `scripts/index.ts`; no other workspace has a tsup config or script |
| `bin` + `files` fields | pointed at `dist/index.js`, which is never built — no `dist/` exists |
| `@clack/prompts`, `commander` | imported only by the deleted CLI files |
| `@auto-it/first-time-contributor` | a plugin for the `auto` release tool, which isn't installed and has no `.autorc` |
| `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/*`, `pull_request_template.md` | the bug report asks "**has-toggle version** — I am using version ...", i.e. addressed at users of the npm package |
| `.github/copilot-instructions.md.example`, `.cursorrules.example` | unfilled `<PROJECT_NAME>` placeholders describing a Prisma/twblocks stack that no longer exists |

Also set the root package `"private": true` — with the `bin` gone, nothing here is publishable, and it shouldn't be.

**Verification:** `turbo build --filter=web` green, 17/17 tasks (test and typecheck are build dependencies, so both ran), 222 web tests pass, `node --check scripts/skip-ci.js` OK, turbo task graph resolves, Biome clean on the changed files. `bun install` removed 4 packages and nothing else.

Docs updated to match: `CLAUDE.md`'s overview no longer describes next-forge's five principles as this project's, its stale "Bundling: tsup for package builds" line now says packages are consumed as TS source through `workspace:*`, and the key-files list names `skip-ci.js` so nobody deletes it next time. The README's next-forge section says what was removed and why `skip-ci.js` wasn't.

**Two things I left alone, for you to call:**
- `esbuild: "0.28.2"` is still in root `overrides`. It was probably there for tsup, but esbuild may still be in the tree via Storybook — removing it is a real risk for no gain, so I didn't.
- `packages/seo/metadata.ts` sets `applicationName = "has-toggle"` and `packages/rate-limit` uses `"has-toggle"` as its Redis key prefix. Those are live runtime values, not dead weight — but the first one reaches page metadata as `has-toggle` rather than `hasToggle`. The rate-limit prefix would need care to change, since it'd reset existing counters.

feat(web): the lab — give every exhibit a home under /lab
=== BODY ===
## What this is

The approved playground architecture (design round 2026-08-20): a serialized web book whose chapters run. One flat contents page at `/lab`, one route segment per chapter at `/lab/<slug>`, all driven by a single syllabus registry. The forcing fact: at least 8 of the 17 upcoming topics are made of routes (parallel/intercepted, not-found, params, view transitions, ISR, navigation…) and cannot live on any single page.

Mid-build scope addition from Eric: the landing page speaks lab vocabulary too — "exhibit" is out of visitor prose everywhere ("chapter" for the unit, "the lab" for the place); it survives as internal working vocabulary in code comments and the design docs.

It kept going from there. The branch is now the pass that brings the rest of the site into the same house grammar — blog, contact, legal, nav, footer — ships chapter 06, and retires the chapter numerals.

## Slices

- [x] 1 — syllabus registry (`lab/syllabus.ts`); contents bar + roadmap derive from it, landing byte-identical (tests pin the old literals)
- [x] 2 — the five demo wrappers extracted into their `(playground)` folders, chapter/topic/belief read from the registry
- [x] 3 — five chapter pages at `/lab/<slug>`: belief as h1, same instrument, making-of aside (folder commit history + checkpoints repo), page-turn (prev · contents · next), per-chapter OG card drawn by `/api/og` from the belief
- [x] 4 — `/lab` contents page (belief-titled rows, lands-Monday row, still-to-build `+` rows, digest capture) + sitemap entries
- [x] 5 — live readings on contents rows (one true value per chapter, each in its own Suspense — the index is itself a PPR demonstration; per-visitor values labeled as yours) + `/latest` → newest chapter
- [x] 6 — lab-vocabulary sweep (landing, FAQ, `/confirmed`, OG card), "A new chapter lands in the lab" re-anchor, contents-bar → The lab link, roadmap → contents link, decisions recorded in voice.md §6 + design.md §4

(3 and 4 were built in swapped order so contents links never 404'd.)

## What landed after those six

**The lab**
- Chapter 06 shipped — useState & re-renders, with the card that turns to its own source and replays the click against it, annotated with values read live (`746fc10c`, `99bdf830`, `b391e71b`, `e066d6ca`, `4c6cc635`).
- The contents page is shelved by section, carved the way the React / Next.js / Vercel docs carve the territory (`8f4c83d3`), and its standfirst states the titling frame once, since an index of beliefs can't explain itself the way a running exhibit does (`7d37a9c3`).
- **The chapter numerals are gone** (`37b61a20`). A number only ever said which week a chapter got built — arbitrary, since the digest extends the syllabus in whatever order the work happens, and there is no chapter 04 in the Next.js or Vercel docs to match it against. The eyebrow names the chapter and its topic instead, anchors key on the slug (`#demo-caching`, which also survives a chapter changing shelves), and the page-turn walks `READING_ORDER` — SECTIONS, then registry order — so the book's spine is the learning arc rather than the build log. The `/lab` row gutter keeps its column and carries a status glyph: a hairline rule for a chapter that is here, a `+` for one that isn't yet.
- The lab headline states the plan rather than naming the bin: **Everything Next.js can do, one chapter at a time.** (`dcb745a6`)
- The state card's face now holds its number for the length of the replay and changes it when the card is square to the reader again, where the digits rise once into place (`fee011ad`, `520c4868`). The state still updates on the click frame; what waits is the display, and the aside's fine print is what states that gap.

**The rest of the site**
- Blog: reskin, standfirst, footer links (`512b57fb`), the article's layout restored and given its voice across five passes (`bca73927`, `2dfa1cda`, `af068009`, `fb66603f`, `8e8790e8`, `4f81178d`), and the index gains per-row thumbnails and the headline **Web development, told as stories.** (`956b02c5`)
- Contact: *Write to Eric* — a Server Action wired straight to an inbox, which is the mutation chapter's lesson doing its day job (`f01d1e5c`); replies come from eric@hastoggle.dev, and every plus in the frame is on the rules (`8d2afed9`).
- Legal: imprint and privacy under German law with real data, terms boilerplate deleted (`231ff07b`, `31959c29`); the demo cookie's stated lifetime is read from the code (`4fe62e7f`).
- One-click unsubscribe — a deletion, not a flag, removed from both stores (`8e84f2ba`).
- Nav: a real top nav for destinations, the theme switcher demoted to a footer pill, dark hover fixed, footer split into two categories and centred in its plus frames (`23e93c0c`, `3a8b71f4`, `2fd639ba`, `015244c6`).
- Route navigations open at the top; the anchor glide stays (`5e08812d`).

**Found on the way**
- `Heading`/`Subheading` called `cn(className, defaults)`, so twMerge resolved every conflict in the component's favour: every `text-balance` and `sm:text-5xl` passed to a Heading had been silently dropped site-wide — headings computed `text-wrap: pretty` and rendered `sm:text-6xl` (`9b6f26e2`). Visible only below `md`, where it was worst: chapter titles rendered 60px through the 640–767px band that asked for 36px.
- That fix made the landing digest eyebrow's cyan effective for the first time, at 3.2:1 on the tinted panel — under AA. It is now `ht-cyan-900`: 6.42:1 light, 9.81:1 dark, measured in the browser against the composited background.
- Biome's `noUnnecessaryConditions` reads `useRef`'s initializer as the whole type, so `if (ref.current)` reports as always falsy. The state cards' seven ref guards now compare explicitly (`2f328049`), and the last three lint errors went with them (`a05a470c`). `biome check` is clean across `apps` and `packages`.
- Housekeeping from the design round, plus the rest: Mintlify starter and `/pricing` removed (`dbd9fe7c`), the qa-stories lesson retired (`2e048e4c`), hello-world dropped and the CLAUDE.md docs block pointed at the bundled Next docs (`2125d057`), `.playwright-mcp` artifacts gitignored (`122c3e26`).

## Verification

Per slice: Biome + tsc + `bun test` in apps/web — **220 passing**, with the registry suite now pinning shelf order and asserting that no entry carries a displayable ordinal. `biome check` clean across apps + packages (472 files).

Production builds after every route-shaped slice: all five chapters prerender for all six locales; `/lab` is ◐ partial-prerender with exactly one per-visitor hole (the press count). `/latest` 307s to the newest chapter; rendered landing has zero "exhibit".

The shared-bake check ran on the Vercel preview per design.md §6, and it found something: **build workers bake `use cache` entries independently**, so the landing shell and `/lab`'s contents row each prerendered their own fingerprint, and a fresh deploy can serve two of them for "one shared entry" until the first tag revalidation or `cacheLife` expiry converges them at runtime. Recorded in design.md §6 (`befb1d3d`); the rule that falls out is that copy must not claim cross-page agreement for the static shells of a fresh deploy.

Browser-verified for the later work: blog thumbnails at 390 and 1280; `/lab`, both ends of the page-turn, and the slug anchors after the numerals came out; the contact aside's link; and the state card's hold-and-settle — a press every 200ms for eight seconds, with the displayed value going 0, 1, 2 and never backwards.

## Follow-ups deliberately not in this PR

- **Open** — the navigation chapter (the one landing next) claims the contents rows' hover-prefetch as its instrument in the site's own chrome. Banked in design.md §5.
- **Open** — chapter-page Lighthouse pass: the `ht-reveal` at the top of a chapter page may want the landing's LCP treatment. Untouched on this branch.
- **Resolved** — the housekeeping this PR surfaced: `apps/docs` (untouched Mintlify starter) and `/pricing` (next-forge placeholder) are deleted (`dbd9fe7c`); `(counter)/` was kept deliberately at first, then superseded and deleted when chapter 06 shipped the same lesson on the instrument grammar (`746fc10c`), with its two revival paths banked in design.md §5.
- **Note, not work** — if Biome's `useRef` inference is fixed upstream, the state cards' explicit `!== null` guards can go back to plain truthiness tests; the comments in both files say why they are written that way.

content.content:
feat(web): the next-up row names the Monday it lands

"lands Monday" was true every day of the week, which made it furniture.
The row now reads "lands Monday · 31 Aug", so a visitor can tell whether
that is five days away or tomorrow.

The date lives in the registry (`lands`, ISO) rather than being derived
from "the next Monday", because it is a commitment, not a calculation: if
a week slips, the row should say the date that was promised instead of
rolling silently to the following one. Promoting a chapter already means
editing its entry, so the date is set where the status is.

Formatted by hand from the ISO parts in UTC, not through Intl — the row is
prerendered, and a date that formats against the server's locale and then
the visitor's is two strings for one static row.

Two tests: the next chapter's date parses as ISO and lands on a Monday,
and the formatter prints the three shapes it has to get right (day of
month with and without a leading digit, and a year boundary).

timeline, per visitor. The site already performs the feature the chapter
will be about, so the instrument exists before the exhibit does.

Keyed by the chapter's slug in INDEX_VALUES, in the chapter's own folder
under (playground)/navigation — the day it ships, the row keeps its
instrument and only the status changes.

Three rules recorded in design.md §4, because "every upcoming chapter
gets a preview" would be the wrong reading of this: it must measure the
running site rather than simulate the chapter, it keys on the slug, and
it stays optional — where nothing true can be read (view transitions,
cron, error recovery) the row is the topic and the date. A slot that must
be filled gets filled with something invented.

The bank note in §5 that asked for this said "hover-prefetch". Building
it disproved that: next/link prefetches on viewport, and five routes were
already fetched before the pointer moved. Also nothing at all in
`next dev`, so this only tells the truth against a production build.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
## What this is

The approved playground architecture (design round 2026-08-20): a serialized web book whose chapters run. One flat contents page at `/lab`, one route segment per chapter at `/lab/<slug>`, all driven by a single syllabus registry. The forcing fact: at least 8 of the 17 upcoming topics are made of routes (parallel/intercepted, not-found, params, view transitions, ISR, navigation…) and cannot live on any single page.

Mid-build scope addition from Eric: the landing page speaks lab vocabulary too — "exhibit" is out of visitor prose everywhere ("chapter" for the unit, "the lab" for the place); it survives as internal working vocabulary in code comments and the design docs.

It kept going from there. The branch is now the pass that brings the rest of the site into the same house grammar — blog, contact, legal, nav, footer — ships chapter 06, and retires the chapter numerals.

## Slices

- [x] 1 — syllabus registry (`lab/syllabus.ts`); contents bar + roadmap derive from it, landing byte-identical (tests pin the old literals)
- [x] 2 — the five demo wrappers extracted into their `(playground)` folders, chapter/topic/belief read from the registry
- [x] 3 — five chapter pages at `/lab/<slug>`: belief as h1, same instrument, making-of aside (folder commit history + checkpoints repo), page-turn (prev · contents · next), per-chapter OG card drawn by `/api/og` from the belief
- [x] 4 — `/lab` contents page (belief-titled rows, lands-Monday row, still-to-build `+` rows, digest capture) + sitemap entries
- [x] 5 — live readings on contents rows (one true value per chapter, each in its own Suspense — the index is itself a PPR demonstration; per-visitor values labeled as yours) + `/latest` → newest chapter
- [x] 6 — lab-vocabulary sweep (landing, FAQ, `/confirmed`, OG card), "A new chapter lands in the lab" re-anchor, contents-bar → The lab link, roadmap → contents link, decisions recorded in voice.md §6 + design.md §4

(3 and 4 were built in swapped order so contents links never 404'd.)

## What landed after those six

**The lab**
- Chapter 06 shipped — useState & re-renders, with the card that turns to its own source and replays the click against it, annotated with values read live (`746fc10c`, `99bdf830`, `b391e71b`, `e066d6ca`, `4c6cc635`).
- The contents page is shelved by section, carved the way the React / Next.js / Vercel docs carve the territory (`8f4c83d3`), and its standfirst states the titling frame once, since an index of beliefs can't explain itself the way a running exhibit does (`7d37a9c3`).
- **The chapter numerals are gone** (`37b61a20`). A number only ever said which week a chapter got built — arbitrary, since the digest extends the syllabus in whatever order the work happens, and there is no chapter 04 in the Next.js or Vercel docs to match it against. The eyebrow names the chapter and its topic instead, anchors key on the slug (`#demo-caching`, which also survives a chapter changing shelves), and the page-turn walks `READING_ORDER` — SECTIONS, then registry order — so the book's spine is the learning arc rather than the build log. The `/lab` row gutter keeps its column and carries a status glyph: a hairline rule for a chapter that is here, a `+` for one that isn't yet.
- The lab headline states the plan rather than naming the bin: **Everything Next.js can do, one chapter at a time.** (`dcb745a6`)
- The state card's face now holds its number for the length of the replay and changes it when the card is square to the reader again, where the digits rise once into place (`fee011ad`, `520c4868`). The state still updates on the click frame; what waits is the display, and the aside's fine print is what states that gap.

**The rest of the site**
- Blog: reskin, standfirst, footer links (`512b57fb`), the article's layout restored and given its voice across five passes (`bca73927`, `2dfa1cda`, `af068009`, `fb66603f`, `8e8790e8`, `4f81178d`), and the index gains per-row thumbnails and the headline **Web development, told as stories.** (`956b02c5`)
- Contact: *Write to Eric* — a Server Action wired straight to an inbox, which is the mutation chapter's lesson doing its day job (`f01d1e5c`); replies come from eric@hastoggle.dev, and every plus in the frame is on the rules (`8d2afed9`).
- Legal: imprint and privacy under German law with real data, terms boilerplate deleted (`231ff07b`, `31959c29`); the demo cookie's stated lifetime is read from the code (`4fe62e7f`).
- One-click unsubscribe — a deletion, not a flag, removed from both stores (`8e84f2ba`).
- Nav: a real top nav for destinations, the theme switcher demoted to a footer pill, dark hover fixed, footer split into two categories and centred in its plus frames (`23e93c0c`, `3a8b71f4`, `2fd639ba`, `015244c6`).
- Route navigations open at the top; the anchor glide stays (`5e08812d`).

**Found on the way**
- `Heading`/`Subheading` called `cn(className, defaults)`, so twMerge resolved every conflict in the component's favour: every `text-balance` and `sm:text-5xl` passed to a Heading had been silently dropped site-wide — headings computed `text-wrap: pretty` and rendered `sm:text-6xl` (`9b6f26e2`). Visible only below `md`, where it was worst: chapter titles rendered 60px through the 640–767px band that asked for 36px.
- That fix made the landing digest eyebrow's cyan effective for the first time, at 3.2:1 on the tinted panel — under AA. It is now `ht-cyan-900`: 6.42:1 light, 9.81:1 dark, measured in the browser against the composited background.
- Biome's `noUnnecessaryConditions` reads `useRef`'s initializer as the whole type, so `if (ref.current)` reports as always falsy. The state cards' seven ref guards now compare explicitly (`2f328049`), and the last three lint errors went with them (`a05a470c`). `biome check` is clean across `apps` and `packages`.
- Housekeeping from the design round, plus the rest: Mintlify starter and `/pricing` removed (`dbd9fe7c`), the qa-stories lesson retired (`2e048e4c`), hello-world dropped and the CLAUDE.md docs block pointed at the bundled Next docs (`2125d057`), `.playwright-mcp` artifacts gitignored (`122c3e26`).

## Verification

Per slice: Biome + tsc + `bun test` in apps/web — **220 passing**, with the registry suite now pinning shelf order and asserting that no entry carries a displayable ordinal. `biome check` clean across apps + packages (472 files).

Production builds after every route-shaped slice: all five chapters prerender for all six locales; `/lab` is ◐ partial-prerender with exactly one per-visitor hole (the press count). `/latest` 307s to the newest chapter; rendered landing has zero "exhibit".

The shared-bake check ran on the Vercel preview per design.md §6, and it found something: **build workers bake `use cache` entries independently**, so the landing shell and `/lab`'s contents row each prerendered their own fingerprint, and a fresh deploy can serve two of them for "one shared entry" until the first tag revalidation or `cacheLife` expiry converges them at runtime. Recorded in design.md §6 (`befb1d3d`); the rule that falls out is that copy must not claim cross-page agreement for the static shells of a fresh deploy.

Browser-verified for the later work: blog thumbnails at 390 and 1280; `/lab`, both ends of the page-turn, and the slug anchors after the numerals came out; the contact aside's link; and the state card's hold-and-settle — a press every 200ms for eight seconds, with the displayed value going 0, 1, 2 and never backwards.

## Follow-ups deliberately not in this PR

- **Open** — the navigation chapter (the one landing next) claims the contents rows' hover-prefetch as its instrument in the site's own chrome. Banked in design.md §5.
- **Open** — chapter-page Lighthouse pass: the `ht-reveal` at the top of a chapter page may want the landing's LCP treatment. Untouched on this branch.
- **Resolved** — the housekeeping this PR surfaced: `apps/docs` (untouched Mintlify starter) and `/pricing` (next-forge placeholder) are deleted (`dbd9fe7c`); `(counter)/` was kept deliberately at first, then superseded and deleted when chapter 06 shipped the same lesson on the instrument grammar (`746fc10c`), with its two revival paths banked in design.md §5.
- **Note, not work** — if Biome's `useRef` inference is fixed upstream, the state cards' explicit `!== null` guards can go back to plain truthiness tests; the comments in both files say why they are written that way.

## What this is

The approved playground architecture (design round 2026-08-20): a serialized web book whose chapters run. One flat contents page at `/lab`, one route segment per chapter at `/lab/<slug>`, all driven by a single syllabus registry. The forcing fact: at least 8 of the 17 upcoming topics are made of routes (parallel/intercepted, not-found, params, view transitions, ISR, navigation…) and cannot live on any single page.

Mid-build scope addition from Eric: the landing page speaks lab vocabulary too — "exhibit" is out of visitor prose everywhere ("chapter" for the unit, "the lab" for the place); it survives as internal working vocabulary in code comments and the design docs.

It kept going from there. The branch is now the pass that brings the rest of the site into the same house grammar — blog, contact, legal, nav, footer — ships chapter 06, retires the chapter numerals, and finishes by making the repo itself describe this site instead of the template it was scaffolded from.

## Slices

- [x] 1 — syllabus registry (`lab/syllabus.ts`); contents bar + roadmap derive from it, landing byte-identical (tests pin the old literals)
- [x] 2 — the five demo wrappers extracted into their `(playground)` folders, chapter/topic/belief read from the registry
- [x] 3 — five chapter pages at `/lab/<slug>`: belief as h1, same instrument, making-of aside (folder commit history + checkpoints repo), page-turn (prev · contents · next), per-chapter OG card drawn by `/api/og` from the belief
- [x] 4 — `/lab` contents page (belief-titled rows, lands-Monday row, still-to-build `+` rows, digest capture) + sitemap entries
- [x] 5 — live readings on contents rows (one true value per chapter, each in its own Suspense — the index is itself a PPR demonstration; per-visitor values labeled as yours) + `/latest` → newest chapter
- [x] 6 — lab-vocabulary sweep (landing, FAQ, `/confirmed`, OG card), "A new chapter lands in the lab" re-anchor, contents-bar → The lab link, roadmap → contents link, decisions recorded in voice.md §6 + design.md §4

(3 and 4 were built in swapped order so contents links never 404'd.)

## What landed after those six

**The lab**
- Chapter 06 shipped — useState & re-renders, with the card that turns to its own source and replays the click against it, annotated with values read live (`746fc10c`, `99bdf830`, `b391e71b`, `e066d6ca`, `4c6cc635`).
- The contents page is shelved by section, carved the way the React / Next.js / Vercel docs carve the territory (`8f4c83d3`), and its standfirst states the titling frame once, since an index of beliefs can't explain itself the way a running exhibit does (`7d37a9c3`).
- **The chapter numerals are gone** (`37b61a20`). A number only ever said which week a chapter got built — arbitrary, since the digest extends the syllabus in whatever order the work happens, and there is no chapter 04 in the Next.js or Vercel docs to match it against. The eyebrow names the chapter and its topic instead, anchors key on the slug (`#demo-caching`, which also survives a chapter changing shelves), and the page-turn walks `READING_ORDER` — SECTIONS, then registry order — so the book's spine is the learning arc rather than the build log. The `/lab` row gutter keeps its column and carries a status glyph: a hairline rule for a chapter that is here, a `+` for one that isn't yet.
- The lab headline states the plan rather than naming the bin: **Everything Next.js can do, one chapter at a time.** (`dcb745a6`)
- The state card's face now holds its number for the length of the replay and changes it when the card is square to the reader again, where the digits rise once into place (`fee011ad`, `520c4868`). The state still updates on the click frame; what waits is the display, and the aside's fine print is what states that gap.

**The rest of the site**
- Blog: reskin, standfirst, footer links (`512b57fb`), the article's layout restored and given its voice across five passes (`bca73927`, `2dfa1cda`, `af068009`, `fb66603f`, `8e8790e8`, `4f81178d`), and the index gains per-row thumbnails and the headline **Web development, told as stories.** (`956b02c5`)
- Contact: *Write to Eric* — a Server Action wired straight to an inbox, which is the mutation chapter's lesson doing its day job (`f01d1e5c`); replies come from eric@hastoggle.dev, and every plus in the frame is on the rules (`8d2afed9`).
- Legal: imprint and privacy under German law with real data, terms boilerplate deleted (`231ff07b`, `31959c29`); the demo cookie's stated lifetime is read from the code (`4fe62e7f`).
- One-click unsubscribe — a deletion, not a flag, removed from both stores (`8e84f2ba`).
- Nav: a real top nav for destinations, the theme switcher demoted to a footer pill, dark hover fixed, footer split into two categories and centred in its plus frames (`23e93c0c`, `3a8b71f4`, `2fd639ba`, `015244c6`).
- Route navigations open at the top; the anchor glide stays (`5e08812d`).

**Found on the way**
- `Heading`/`Subheading` called `cn(className, defaults)`, so twMerge resolved every conflict in the component's favour: every `text-balance` and `sm:text-5xl` passed to a Heading had been silently dropped site-wide — headings computed `text-wrap: pretty` and rendered `sm:text-6xl` (`9b6f26e2`). Visible only below `md`, where it was worst: chapter titles rendered 60px through the 640–767px band that asked for 36px.
- That fix made the landing digest eyebrow's cyan effective for the first time, at 3.2:1 on the tinted panel — under AA. It is now `ht-cyan-900`: 6.42:1 light, 9.81:1 dark, measured in the browser against the composited background.
- Biome's `noUnnecessaryConditions` reads `useRef`'s initializer as the whole type, so `if (ref.current)` reports as always falsy. The state cards' seven ref guards now compare explicitly (`2f328049`), and the last three lint errors went with them (`a05a470c`). `biome check` is clean across `apps` and `packages`.
- Housekeeping from the design round, plus the rest: Mintlify starter and `/pricing` removed (`dbd9fe7c`), the qa-stories lesson retired (`2e048e4c`), hello-world dropped and the CLAUDE.md docs block pointed at the bundled Next docs (`2125d057`), `.playwright-mcp` artifacts gitignored (`122c3e26`).

## Verification

Per slice: Biome + tsc + `bun test` in apps/web — **220 passing**, with the registry suite now pinning shelf order and asserting that no entry carries a displayable ordinal. `biome check` clean across apps + packages (472 files).

Production builds after every route-shaped slice: all five chapters prerender for all six locales; `/lab` is ◐ partial-prerender with exactly one per-visitor hole (the press count). `/latest` 307s to the newest chapter; rendered landing has zero "exhibit".

The shared-bake check ran on the Vercel preview per design.md §6, and it found something: **build workers bake `use cache` entries independently**, so the landing shell and `/lab`'s contents row each prerendered their own fingerprint, and a fresh deploy can serve two of them for "one shared entry" until the first tag revalidation or `cacheLife` expiry converges them at runtime. Recorded in design.md §6 (`befb1d3d`); the rule that falls out is that copy must not claim cross-page agreement for the static shells of a fresh deploy.

Browser-verified for the later work: blog thumbnails at 390 and 1280; `/lab`, both ends of the page-turn, and the slug anchors after the numerals came out; the contact aside's link; and the state card's hold-and-settle — a press every 200ms for eight seconds, with the displayed value going 0, 1, 2 and never backwards.

## Follow-ups deliberately not in this PR

- **Open** — the navigation chapter (the one landing next) claims the contents rows' hover-prefetch as its instrument in the site's own chrome. Banked in design.md §5.
- **Open** — chapter-page Lighthouse pass: the `ht-reveal` at the top of a chapter page may want the landing's LCP treatment. Untouched on this branch.
- **Resolved** — the housekeeping this PR surfaced: `apps/docs` (untouched Mintlify starter) and `/pricing` (next-forge placeholder) are deleted (`dbd9fe7c`); `(counter)/` was kept deliberately at first, then superseded and deleted when chapter 06 shipped the same lesson on the instrument grammar (`746fc10c`), with its two revival paths banked in design.md §5.
- **Note, not work** — if Biome's `useRef` inference is fixed upstream, the state cards' explicit `!== null` guards can go back to plain truthiness tests; the comments in both files say why they are written that way.

**The repo describes this site now**

- **The README was untouched next-forge boilerplate** — an install command that doesn't apply, a Mintlify docs app that isn't there, "type-safe ORM with migrations" for a repo that uses the raw MongoDB driver, demo links to `demo.next-forge.com`, and a contributors image for vercel/next-forge. - **"Fork" was the wrong word** (`358fb941`). A fork shares history and has an upstream; `npx next-forge init` copies the template and runs a fresh `git init`. The history starts at Eric's own initial commit, there is no upstream remote, and nothing here gets pulled from it.
- **The template's own repo furniture is gone** (`23f2fb4a`). The scaffold copied next-forge's published npm package into this repo: an `init`/`update` CLI that clones next-forge and migrates between its versions, the tsup build that ships it, a `bin` pointing at a `dist/` that is never built, and issue templates asking which version of the package you're on. Removed with it: `@clack/prompts`, `commander`, `tsup`, `@auto-it/first-time-contributor` (a plugin for a release tool that isn't installed), and two unfilled agent-instruction examples still describing a Prisma stack. The root package is `private` now, since nothing here is published.
  - **`scripts/skip-ci.js` stays.** Deleting `scripts/` wholesale would have taken it, and all four apps' `vercel.json` name it as their Ignored Build Step. Verified before the delete, not after.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/eric/.claude/skills/merging-branches-safely

# Merging Branches Safely

## Overview

Investigate merges **before** touching the working tree. Use `git merge-tree` to predict conflicts without mutating state, classify each conflict, surface a resolution proposal, and only run `git merge` / `git rebase` after the user approves — or immediately if preflight predicts no conflicts.

**Core primitive:** `git merge-tree A B` simulates a full merge and prints conflict markers. No index, worktree, or HEAD changes. It is the single most important tool in this skill.

**Announce at start:** "Using merging-branches-safely — starting with read-only preflight."

## The Four Phases

```dot
digraph merge_flow {
    preflight [shape=box, label="Phase 1: Preflight (read-only)"];
    predicted [shape=diamond, label="merge-tree predicts conflicts?"];
    classify [shape=box, label="Phase 2: Classify + propose"];
    approved [shape=diamond, label="User approves resolution?"];
    execute [shape=box, label="Phase 3: Execute merge/rebase\n+ verify"];
    commit [shape=box, label="Phase 4: Commit (no push)"];
    revise [shape=box, label="Revise proposal"];

    preflight -> predicted;
    predicted -> classify [label="yes"];
    predicted -> execute [label="no"];
    classify -> approved;
    approved -> revise [label="no"];
    revise -> classify;
    approved -> execute [label="yes"];
    execute -> commit;
}
```

### Phase 1 — Preflight (ALWAYS, read-only)

Never start a merge/rebase before this phase completes. Collect, without mutating state:

```bash
# Fork point
BASE=$(git merge-base <ours> <theirs>)

# What each side added
git log --oneline <theirs> ^<ours>          # incoming commits
git log --oneline <ours> ^<theirs>          # our commits

# File-level scope
git diff --stat $BASE..<ours>
git diff --stat $BASE..<theirs>

# Overlap set — files touched on both sides
comm -12 \
  <(git diff --name-only $BASE..<ours> | sort) \
  <(git diff --name-only $BASE..<theirs> | sort)

# Conflict prediction (merge)
git merge-tree <ours> <theirs> 2>&1 | grep -E "^CONFLICT|^Auto-merging"

# Conflict prediction (rebase) — simulate each commit replaying
for sha in $(git log --reverse --format=%H $BASE..<theirs>); do
  git merge-tree <ours> $sha | grep "^CONFLICT" && echo "  ^ at $sha"
done
```

Report to the user: incoming commits, scope, overlap, predicted conflicts (or "none").

If no conflicts predicted → skip to Phase 3.

### Phase 2 — Classify + propose (only when conflicts predicted)

For every overlapping file (conflicting **and** auto-merging), inspect both sides' diffs:

```bash
git diff $BASE..<ours>   -- <path>
git diff $BASE..<theirs> -- <path>
```

Tag each file with one of:

| Tag | Meaning | Default resolution |
|---|---|---|
| `orthogonal` | Both sides edit the same region with semantically independent changes (e.g., one adds an import, one adds a different import nearby) | Combine both |
| `supersede` | One side's change replaces the other's intent (e.g., feature deleted a function main renamed) | Take the winning side and justify |
| `semantic-overlap` | Both sides modify the same behavior — no mechanical answer | Escalate: present options, let user pick |
| `silent-semantic` | Git reports a **clean auto-merge** but the combined code is broken (renamed identifier still referenced, type contract mismatched, invariant violated) | Flag and propose fix — these are the dangerous ones |
| `generated-artifact` | A conflict in a file produced from source, not hand-authored — `pnpm-lock.yaml`, other lockfiles, generated schemas/types | Don't resolve the artifact. Resolve its **source** (the `package.json` files), then **regenerate** it — see Phase 3 |

Auto-merged files still need a classification. `silent-semantic` only surfaces if you look. Skipping this check is the most common failure mode.

**Stop and ask.** Present:
- Per-file tag + proposed resolution (one line each)
- Any `silent-semantic` flags prominently
- A single "approve / change / abort" question

Wait for approval. Do not start the merge.

### Phase 3 — Execute (only after approval, or immediately if Phase 1 was clean)

```bash
git merge <theirs> --no-commit --no-ff   # or: git rebase <theirs>
```

For each conflicting file, apply the approved resolution with the Edit tool (not by hand-rewriting full files).

**`pnpm-lock.yaml` (and any `generated-artifact`) is the exception — never Edit it.** It is generated from the `package.json` files. Resolve every conflicting `package.json` first, **merging both sides' intent** — main's dependency changes *and* the branch's — not one side wholesale. Then discard the conflicted lockfile and regenerate it:

```bash
# Pick the lockfile side that has been re-resolved more recently:
#   merge (main into branch): git checkout --theirs  → uses main's lockfile
#   rebase (branch onto main): git checkout --ours   → also main's lockfile (rebase inverts the semantics)
# Either way, you want main's transitive baseline — Renovate keeps it fresh.
git checkout --theirs pnpm-lock.yaml
pnpm install --lockfile-only --recursive --ignore-scripts --ignore-pnpmfile
pnpm dedupe --ignore-scripts         # only if the repo dedupes its lockfile (check renovate.json5 postUpdateOptions)
git add pnpm-lock.yaml
```

**Side choice matters.** `pnpm install --lockfile-only` is conservative — it keeps every transitive resolution that still satisfies the merged manifests' ranges. If the *branch* side is stale, its older (sometimes vulnerable) transitives still satisfy the caret ranges, so they survive regen + dedupe. Starting from main's lockfile gives pnpm the freshest baseline to reconcile against. `pnpm dedupe` consolidates duplicates but **does not** upgrade resolutions — it cannot fix this on its own. OSV scans on the PR will surface the resulting vulnerability delta against main if you pick the wrong side.

For the full command matrix — lockfile-only-update PRs, `lockFileMaintenance` PRs, the verify-the-bump-landed grep — see `rebasing-renovate-prs-locally`, the specialization for when the whole PR *is* a dependency bump.

Then:

```bash
# Re-verify no markers remain
grep -rn "^<<<<<<< \|^======= $\|^>>>>>>> " <touched-paths>

# Also open each auto-merged overlap file and confirm semantics
# (silent-semantic hides here — auto-merge being clean is not a safety check)

# Run project verification
<project-typecheck-command>
<project-test-command-if-user-has-that-convention>

# If the merge touched package.json / pnpm-lock.yaml: typecheck + test are NOT enough.
# A re-resolved dependency tree can break the bundler only. Also run:
<project-build-command>
pnpm deps:lint                       # syncpack — catches override/specifier drift
```

If verification fails, fix before committing. Never `--no-verify` to ship a broken merge.

### Phase 4 — Commit (never push)

```bash
git add <resolved-paths>
git commit --no-edit          # merge message pre-filled; rebase: git rebase --continue
```

Stop here. Pushing is a separate user-authorized action.

## Guardrails

- **Never `git merge --abort` as an exploration tool.** That's what `git merge-tree` is for. Aborting after a partial merge loses signal and adds noise to the reflog.
- **Never start a merge/rebase before Phase 1.**
- **Never use `-X ours`, `-X theirs`, or `--no-verify` to skip resolution.** They hide conflicts; they don't resolve them.
- **Dirty working tree at Phase 1 → stop and surface.** Do not stash silently; the user may have in-progress work.
- **Auto-merge clean ≠ semantically clean.** Every overlap file gets a tag, including auto-merged ones.
- **Never Edit `pnpm-lock.yaml` (or any generated artifact) to resolve a conflict.** It's derived from the manifests — fix those, then regenerate. A hand-merged lockfile drifts from what the resolver produces and breaks `--frozen-lockfile` installs.
- **One tag per file, written down.** Forces naming before fixing.
- **The approval gate is bypassable in two cases:** (1) Phase 1 predicts zero conflicts, or (2) the user has given explicit pre-authorization in this turn (e.g., "merge and commit, no need to confirm"). Absent either, pause. A generic "merge X into Y" does not count as pre-authorization — users often expect to see the preflight before resolution begins.

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Why it fails | Do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Running `git merge` to "see what conflicts" | Mutates state; forces `--abort`; pollutes reflog | Use `git merge-tree` — zero side effects |
| Skipping auto-merged files in Phase 2 | `silent-semantic` conflicts hide here | Every overlap file gets a tag |
| Resolving before user approval | Treats "merge branch X" as resolution authorization | Approval gate is mandatory when conflicts are predicted |
| Inferring conflict type from the conflict markers alone | Markers show syntax, not intent — you need each side's diff from the merge base | `git diff $BASE..<ours> -- <path>` and the same for theirs |
| Skipping typecheck/tests before commit | Leaves broken merges as commits | Run the project's verification command; if it fails, fix before committing |
| Hand-resolving `pnpm-lock.yaml` conflict markers | Produces a lockfile no resolver would generate; `--frozen-lockfile` installs break | Resolve the `package.json` files, then regenerate the lockfile (Phase 3) |
| Only typecheck/test after a dep-touching merge | Bundler-only breakage (missing transitive export, etc.) passes both | Also run the build + `pnpm deps:lint` when the merge changed dependencies |
| Pushing after committing | User didn't ask for that | Stop at Phase 4; push is a separate ask |

## Quick Reference

**Merge command recipe (after approval):**
```bash
git merge main --no-commit --no-ff
# ... apply per-file resolutions via Edit tool ...
# pnpm-lock.yaml: do NOT Edit — resolve the package.json files, then regenerate (Phase 3)
grep -rn '^<<<<<<< \|^>>>>>>> ' <touched-paths>   # expect no output
<typecheck>   # + build & pnpm deps:lint if deps changed
git add <resolved-paths>
git commit --no-edit
```

**Rebase recipe (after approval):**
```bash
git rebase <target>
# per commit that conflicts:
#   - apply resolution via Edit
#   - git add <paths>
#   - git rebase --continue
<typecheck>   # after the whole rebase finishes
```

**Resuming an in-progress merge you didn't start:** treat the current state as mid-Phase-3. Run `git status` to find unmerged paths, then loop back to Phase 2 on those files: read each side's diff from merge base, tag, propose, wait for approval — don't resolve blind.

## Red Flags — Stop and Restart the Phase

- About to run `git merge` / `git rebase` without having run `git merge-tree` → back to Phase 1
- About to resolve conflicts without having surfaced tags + proposal → back to Phase 2
- Auto-merged file not classified → back to Phase 2
- About to commit without running project verification → back to Phase 3
- About to Edit `pnpm-lock.yaml` or another generated artifact to clear conflict markers → stop; resolve its source and regenerate (Phase 3)
- About to push → stop; that's not this skill's job

content.text:
Merged and committed as `65626f9d`. Working tree clean, no merge state left, **not pushed** — that's a separate call.

**What main brought:** 10 Renovate commits (#385–#401), nothing but dependency bumps across 23 manifests.

**Both conflicts resolved as approved:**

`package.json` — combined both sides. The file keeps our deletions (`bin`, `files`, the `dependencies` block, `@auto-it/first-time-contributor`, `tsup`) and takes main's three bumps: `@biomejs/biome` 2.5.10, `turbo` 2.10.12, and the `@types/react-dom` override at 19.2.5 (that one auto-merged).

`bun.lock` — never edited. Took main's lockfile as the baseline, then regenerated from the merged manifests with `bun install`. Worth noting what that produced: `@clack/prompts` and `commander` are still in the lock, but only as transitives of `ultracite`, which depends on both — the root workspace block lists neither, and `tsup` and `@auto-it/first-time-contributor` are gone entirely. That's the correct outcome, and it's the kind of thing a hand-merged lockfile gets wrong.

**Verification — the flagged risk didn't bite.** `turbo build --filter=web` 17/17 green (test and typecheck run as build dependencies), 222 web tests pass, and `biome check` is clean across 473 files under the bumped 2.5.10. The Biome bump landing on 51 commits of new code was the one thing git couldn't see; it's clear.

One thing the merge quietly brought in that's worth your eye: **Next.js went 16.3.1 → 16.3.3** across the apps. The build and tests pass, but this branch is unusually sensitive to Next's cache and prerender behavior, and per `design.md` §6 a local build doesn't prove cache semantics. The preview deploy after you push is the real check on the rebake flow.

**The rebake flow is intact on Next 16.3.3.** The badge sequence matches `design.md` §6 exactly, step for step:

| Step | Expected (design.md §6) | Observed |
|---|---|---|
| First visit | `PRERENDER` | `PRERENDER` |
| Reload | `HIT` | `HIT`, age 40 |
| Action POST | `BYPASS` | `BYPASS`, plus `x-action-revalidated: 1` |
| Refill | `REVALIDATED` | `REVALIDATED` |

The fingerprint went `b2aa27` → `4a3faa` on the press, and a separate cold fetch — no client state, fresh request — returned `#4a3faa` at `x-vercel-cache: HIT`. So the tag deletion emptied the shelf, the next request baked one copy, and that copy is what everyone gets. `updateTag` still never produces `STALE`, and the miss still files as `REVALIDATED`, not `MISS`.

**But I tested production, not the preview.** The preview is SSO-walled — `curl` gets a 302 to `vercel.com/sso-api`, the MCP browser landed on the Vercel login page, and `web_fetch_vercel_url` couldn't mint a shareable URL either.

Production is a legitimate stand-in for the thing I actually flagged. The Next bump came *from* main, so production is already on 16.3.3, and `bake.ts`, `actions.ts` and `rebake-state.ts` are byte-identical between main and this branch — the branch only touched `demo.tsx` (the extracted wrapper), the new `index-value.tsx`, and two contrast one-liners. The cache mechanism I just exercised is the same code the branch ships.

**What's still unverified, and needs the preview:**
- `/lab/caching` — the chapter page's own wiring of the instrument.
- `ShellIndexValue` on `/lab` — the bake reading on the contents row.

Merging main again re-opens the same race — the lockfile will conflict again the next time a bump lands, and each round costs a full rebuild and another preview deploy.

Two options:

2. **Leave it and resolve once, immediately before merging the PR.** The conflict is confined to a generated file with a deterministic resolution, so there's no review value in keeping the branch continuously current — and every round of this adds a merge commit that says nothing.

I'd go with 2 unless you want the preview deploy green for review right now, in which case 1. Which?
